Many people interested in Japanese RPG's have probably already heard of Nier. In Japan, it has developed a bit of a cult following, thanks to its originality. This game is a bit of an oddity, it is mostly a traditional action-RPG, similar to Demon's Souls or Zelda, with elements of other genres thrown in. Nier sold far better in Japan than it did in the United States, however, there were also two versions of the game released in that territory, Gestalt and Replicant. The States got the Gestalt version with its older protagonist. The States also did not get the accompanying book, Grimoire Nier, which was released only in Japan.

Story: The initial story of Nier involves a disease called the Black Scrawl, which is always fatal. The main protagonist, Nier, has a daughter who contracted the illness. During the first part of the game, it is all about curing her, the second half is in finding her. To help Nier on his quest are three companions, Grimoire Weiss, Kaine, and Emil. Nier himself is a father willing to do anything to get his daughter back, even if it involves killing nearly everything in sight. Grimoire Weiss is a talking book that does nothing but complain and provide insight on what is happening. Kaine is actually a kind-hearted woman who has that part of her shrouded in coarseness, with a very, very thick layer vulgarity and anger to keep others at bay. Emil is a young boy whose only desire is to fix his eyes, which turns everything he looks at to stone. All of these characters help Nier fight Shades, the eerie antagonists who seem to do nothing but attack any human.

Nier's story is exceptionally dark and quite depressing at times. The story is a bit unusual in that you must play through the game four times to see all of the endings. Thankfully, you don't have to restart from the beginning, but only from the second half which can be played through in about three hours, longer if you want to tackle side missions. During the first playthrough, you are focused on finding Nier's daughter and cutting down any Shade getting between you and her. During the second playthrough, you get to see what the Shades are actually saying along with specific stories surrounding individual Shades Nier must fight. The remaining two playthroughs are identical to the second with only the last scenes being different.

Gameplay: Nier is a bit of a mixed bag of play styles, it is a generic hack-and-slash primarily, but it is also a top-down RPG, side scroller, and text-based adventure at other times. Some of the games more interesting moments are during the text-based portion, it adds more depth to the game. This section also is a little humorous since Grimoire Weiss tries to argue with the narrator for using Weiss instead of the full name, the narrator then proceeds to lightly insult him throughout that section. The hack-and slash portion is fairly standard, once you figure out the fighting mechanics and decide on a main weapon, in my case, spears, the game becomes a bit of a button masher. Luckily, there are few areas where you are required to fight to proceed with the story, usually, you can simply race past the enemies should you choose not to. Grimoire Weiss allows Nier to cast spells, and during the second portion of the game, Emil and Kaine join Nier in battle, though, you only get experience points in battle for enemies Nier has defeated directly.

As Nier is an RPG, there are magical elements, quests, and even fishing thrown in. This is a game where language is powerful, it is seen in the music and in the magic. Words can be combined and attached to weapons and spells to increase various stats, magic animations hold the magical energy together with words. Even when shades are defeated you hear ghostly, indecipherable words being spoke. Nier himself has a number of spells that can be used, ranging from orbiting spears, to giant lances, to ghosts of Nier attacking enemies. The quests are very similar and rarely vary from shopping and gathering quests, to fighting quests. There are a few that are different, such as the lighthouse lady quests, but most are the same thing, over, and over again. The fishing and cultivation mini-games are mostly a way to earn additional cash and involve luck or simply waiting for stuff to grow. Once Nier has obtained weapons, he can upgrade them at a shop using various materials he finds and funds he gets from quests.

Audio/Video: Graphics-wise, Nier is a bit disappointing. The graphics are decent, but the lighting effects make everything seem muddy. The weather effects do not help this at all since dust or fog absorb light even more. The character designs are quite nice, Nier himself does take the award for being one of the ugliest characters in the game. Also, the character model borrows from Nier Replicant, which had a younger protagonist, making the much older, in the U.S. version, Nier move a little oddly times. Kaine wears stilettos and not much else, but the outfit is... interesting. Emil's outfit is initially standard, but in the second half, it is suitably creepy and intricate. Environments have that post-apocalyptic feel to them, which is suitable since humanity is facing extinction.

The audio in Nier is absolutely outstanding. The voice actors do their jobs quite well. The music is very, very good. Nier's soundtrack rivals almost any other video game, even Final Fantasy. Language takes center stage in this game, even in the music. There are a handful of different themes, mostly vocal, but they vary quite a bit with additional instruments. In many of the songs, there is a single person performing the piece. Most of those titles are written and performed by Emi Evans, including the game's final theme, "Ashes of Dreams." Ashes is performed four times, one for each ending, each in a different language, English, French, Japanese, and Gaelic. As a side note, the soundtrack lists the Gaelic version as GER, which many believe is German, Emi Evans confirmed there is no German anywhere on the soundtrack. Aside from Ashes, none of the songs are performed in an understandable language, Evans took those four languages, twisted them, combined them, and then created songs with words that simply sound nice. I cannot recommend Nier's soundtrack highly enough, it is a must listen. Top songs include, "Ashes of Dreams," most of the "Song of the Ancients" mixes, Kaine's themes, Emil's themes, and the various forms of Yonah.

Misc.: Nier was an interesting experience, the gameplay wasn't complex, but the story was quite intriguing. The action RPG portion of the game is not very deep, nor is the game crushingly difficult to play, such as Demon's Souls. The graphics are a bit sub-par, but great games should rarely be considered as such solely on eye candy. The story was fascinating, more so after completing the game the first time and seeing where the Shades come from and what they are saying. In many cases, viewing the individual stories of the boss Shades made the battles from the first playthrough tragic in subsequent playthroughs. Indeed, some of the battles went from taking down the evil Shade the first time, to a series of unfortunate misunderstandings that led to battle in the second, third, and fourth plays of the game. In fact, some of them actually made me a bit misty-eyed, like the one between P-33 (a.k.a. Beepy) and Roc (a.k.a. The Shade Wolf). Nier's saving grace comes from the originality, few games take the risk of adding in a text-driven adventure game to the middle of a hack-and-slash, nor do they add side-scrollers. Few games rarely have the caliber of audio Nier has, even most AAA titles.

Overall, I enjoyed my experience with Nier. The game world isn't too large, but that means the areas can be relatively rich with content. The main story is original, though very depressing at times, but the side missions lack variety. The art design in some cases is quite inventive, especially those involving characters or enemies, but it gets bogged down by lighting effects that make everything seem muddy. The game has different modes of play which allow it to take a breather from the standard action RPG model. As for trophies, this game is mostly about gathering and grinding. A few trophies do require skill, but during multiple playthrough's, those are going to be quite easy given how powerful Nier will become. The weapon upgrading trophies will be difficult to earn, only because of the patience involved in doing them, same is true with the money-earning trophy. One of the more difficult trophies will involve completing the game within a certain amount of time. The player will have to race to get it done fast enough. Nier will very much be a niche title, appealing to those who like Japanese RPG's first and foremost, people who like action RPG's but don't necessarily like JRPG's, may want to consider renting this before purchasing. Given how the story evolved, it is possible to create a Nier 2, but it is far from certain that Square Enix will want to do this especially with the game's developer, Cavia, being disbanded. It would be in Square Enix's best interest if they could get the game's composers to do more titles, such as Final Fantasy, to truly showcase their masterful work. This is a game that doesn't do anything remarkable, gameplay wise, but it is still fun.

I got this game over the holidays after hearing reviews and weighing the pro's and con's. Many of the reviews agree that it is a fairly generic platformer and adventure title, but the music and art direction were top notch with an unusual story. Considering I played and liked the critically panned, but cult favorite, "Nier", I thought I would give this a try.

El Shaddai is indeed an easy game to get into thanks to its easy-to-use controls, the art and music were very much top-notch, but after a while, the problems began. Initially, I discovered that I wasn't supposed to defeat certain fallen angels but to be defeated and mocked by them. This wasn't fully explained but I wrote it off as a story choice and didn't put up much of a fight the next time one rolled around. The side scrolling platforming elements were indeed clever, but the artwork can be a hinderance. The controls, though easy to pick up and learn, are very sensitive and I found myself falling all over the maps thanks to this and the camera.

Controls for the game are easy to figure out, you just need to press a given button at a fast or slow rate, you can also hold down the attack button for more power. The camera isn't mapped to the right stick so you are at the mercy of the game for camera control. The voice over work is well done, but lip syncing is off. With the removal of a HUD, you must watch Enoch, the main character, to see how close to death he is based on the armor. You can die in battle, but if you hit every button on the controller, you resurrect, however, if you fall off the map too many times, it is game over and you have to reload.

As the game progressed, it went from tolerating the problems to becoming frustrated by design decisions. The overly sensitive controls become a greater liability as the game progresses and you have to make finer and finer jumps. By the time chapter eight rolled around, I had enough, the art on that level made it nearly impossible to see where I was going, the controls sent me flying off into oblivion dozens of times, there was no ability for me to adjust the camera for greater control, and I had no idea where I was supposed to be going. By this point, the good parts of the game, the art, the clever level design, the simplicity, had worn off completely and I was contemplating selling the game.

If you are expecting a diamond in the rough, there is one here, but it is only so good. The art and music are fantastic and the story elements are rarely done in video games. However, the controls made the game a pain to play, the enemies are all the same only with varying levels of armor, art direction often trumps game design, and getting all the trophies is nearly impossible. This is not a "Nier" experience, which I still think back fondly on months later despite the faults. If you can put up with the faults, the game can shine, but if you discover yourself merely tolerating design elements early on, it will get worse.

So please, quit the whining and Capcom bashing already, it seems like a fair system. If you are poor and don't have much money Capcom did you a favor by cheapening the price of initial play. I might get rate downs for saying it but it's how it is.
As for the game itself, I feared it would be a rehashed SF4 with some Tekken characters thrown in. In actuality, even from the opening cinematic, you begin to understand that SF X Tekken is a little different lol. It is a game that seems like it was made purely for fun and the whimsy of it begins to shine through constantly. You can also tell that something else is a little different, now there is a team angle. Which is where things begin to get really interesting. You can tell Capcom had a chance to play Super Smash Brothers and also observe some RPG teamwork abilities since SF4 came out. The differences made to SF X Tekken are subtle, yet begin to really grow on you over time.
Let me say that it is pretty much awesome to have a team situation where you can call in the other character.. who is the other player on your team. Soon, you find yourself pacing out the fight and juggling with wise meter use. The meter suddenly becomes a vaguely "TP" (haha FFXI) like source that you can use to either spam individual skills or save for skillchain team attack sequences, which look AWESOME. Team play, yes, does continue into the online battles which vastly changes the dynamic and indeed seems like tons of fun. Online battles are very fair, with a very good ability match search.
Once again, I want to mention the whimsy of SF X Tekken. It is very noticeable and fun, from the whimsical, humorous happenings in the backgrounds, the character phrasings, the music and even the battle system. You get a sense that Capcom has realized the need to get younger players on board and that those SF Alpha players now have a family to raise. Hopefully, Capcom has a new and or refreshed Megaman series in the works, with Roll, Wily and the bots.
Pretty good, seems like the SF4 engine days might be coming to an end and SF X Tekken is a good way to end it!

I've been playing with my Wii Fit system for over a month now and I still don't feel like I've tapped in to everything it has to offer! First of all, let me make it clear that if you're in good shape and used to doing reasonably intense exercise most days, the Wii Fit will not be able to replace your current workout, it's just not intense enough. It can, however, be a fun way to supplement your workout with some bonus exercise!

If you're just starting out, the Wii Fit is probably a great place to start. You can do it in the privacy of your own home (great for people who don't want to join classes at a public gym), but with the balance board and remote, it's more interactive than, say, doing a workout video. The system is able to test your speed and form as you go along, which makes it harder to slack off during your workout. The exercises get harder as you get better at them, which means you can improve at your own pace.

The Wii Fit offers five areas of exercise:

1. Aerobic exercises: Exercises designed to get your heart rate up and burn calories. These aren't very intense, but the hula hooping one is a blast, and works the muscles in my back like no other exercise I've ever found. Most of the exercises are variations on classic step aerobics.

2. Strength training exercises: Exercises that tone and strengthen your muscles, mostly classic moves like squats and curls. Using the remote, these aren't very challenging if you have any muscle at all, but you can make them more difficult if you have a basic set of hand weights.

3. Yoga: Exercises to stretch your muscles and improve your posture. These are GREAT for doing after a workout to stretch, and they really do help you relax. The balance board allows you to check your form better than if you're trying to follow a yoga DVD.

4. Balance games: Exercises that test your body control by making you shift your weight around to accomplish certain tasks. These are the least calorie-burning but the most fun, and they're still better for you than sitting on the couch with a movie all evening.

5. Wii Fit Plus exercises: These are just a combination of new games they've come up with since the last version of the Wii Fit. Most of them are balance games, but again, they're really fun. The balance board adds a level of interaction that you don't get with most video games.

In addition, the game allows you to track your progress with body tests that check your weight and balance, and allows you to set goals and watch your progress toward reaching them. You can also create your own customized workouts using exercises from the system, so that you can run through them all seamlessly without having to individually select each activity.

So here's the bottom line: If you're a beginner, the Wii Fit Plus can be a great way to jump start your weight loss goals. If you're a seasoned health buff, you'll still find things to like about the Wii Fit even if it's not your main workout. At the end of the day, it's still just what the Wii is all about: a really fun game.

Since I never played the first Scribblenauts game, I didn't know what to expect when I ordered this one. I'm happy with what I got! I had hoped for a game with a central storyline, where I would be progressing through increasingly difficult levels by conjuring up objects to help me along the way. It turned out that wasn't the case at all, this game is just a big collection of unrelated puzzles, with easy and difficult ones all jumbled together. Once I got over this initial disappointment, I had a lot of fun with it.

Basically the idea is that for each puzzle, you have to create objects to accomplish a certain task. For instance, you might have to come up with something that will put an angry lion to sleep, cause a dinosaur extinction, or appease a hungry bear. You may also have to conjure objects that you can perform actions with, like a car to drive or a shovel to dig with. You also might have to use adjectives to complete a puzzle, like populating a scene with scary horror monsters by creating an "evil puppy" or a "zombie giraffe." The game will produce (nearly) anything your brain can come up with, so you can go as mundane or wild as you want with it. This is strictly a puzzle game, so if you're looking for heavy action, look elsewhere.

Pros:
-Super creative gameplay makes this a nice change from typical puzzle games that only have one correct answer to each puzzle
-Most levels can be replayed in "challenge" mode where you have to solve the same puzzle with three different solutions. Most puzzles have one obvious solution, but coming up with three is a real challenge in some cases.
-Different types of levels keeps gameplay diverse enough to be interesting. Some levels may require you to analyze similarities between objects to come up with parallel objects, some levels require you to navigate an obstacle course, and some require you to interact with other characters or creatures in some way. Some are extremely easy while some truly stretch your imagination!
-The "hints" system is just right, giving you a few nudges in the right direction when you need them without actually solving the puzzles for you
-Most of the puzzles are untimed, so you're limited only by your own creativity!

Cons:
-While you can conjure anything you want, the objects don't always behave in the way you expect. I conjured up a hypnotist to put a lion to sleep, but he just wandered around aimlessly.
-The game is strangely picky about which solutions it will accept sometimes. Occasionally it will accept one phrase, but not another that means exactly the same thing.
-The keyboard you use to name objects is over-sensitive. I was constantly having to backspace when it entered a letter twice.
-A lot of the puzzles have very similar solutions. A lot of them can be solved through a combination of jet packs, potions, and explosives.
-Like I said, this game is just a series of short puzzles with nothing really tying them together. This makes it a great game to just pick up and play for a few minutes here and there, but it also means it can tend to get dull quickly.
-The game doesn't seem to get progressively difficult. I would have liked it better if it started easy and got harder as you went along instead of hard and easy puzzles just being all mixed up together.

Overall, this game was a lot of fun and I can see myself going back to replay it many times. It's a must-buy for everyone who adores puzzle games!

I was really excited for the remake of Final Fantasy VII, but this game kind of feels like a chore to play through... I’m about 15 hours into the game and debating if I want to continue or not.

So, first of all the graphics are great! Nice to see everything updated; they did an excellent job!

The other part that seems well done is the character development. You get a lot more backstory on some of the characters you didn’t really get to know as well in the original (as well as the ones you did).

I don’t think you would like this game if you haven’t played the original, though. The story is way too stretched out... doesn’t really work as a stand alone unless you already know the story.

Seems like there is a lot of fluff. Like a lot of needless walking... Some needless story... Some story that really doesn’t make sense.

Some people may like the battle system, but I was not a big fan. A huge part of the original game was the battle system, and that is completely different in this game; it’s more like an action/adventure game. They try to mix that with issuing commands, but it just doesn’t feel right. That said, you can get used to it... it’s just not all that fun.

Also, normal mode seems a little difficult to me (with battles that take forever), and easy mode seems way too easy, so it just wasn’t a good fit for me.

If you’re a diehard fan, you should definitely give this one a try, but just know that it’s not the original game; it’s a remake with tons of filler and a different battle system, which you may either find to be refreshing or a chore to play through.

This game is absolutely perfect in many regards. The graphics are crisp; the storyline is funny; the dungeons are well-designed; the music is great; there are lots of fun collection opportunities.

But there’s one thing that completely breaks the game for me, and that is the battle system. So, at the end of battle you don’t get experience points (etc.). You just get coins... which is pointless because you have about 5,000 coins saved up within the first 30 minutes of the game. There really is no reward for doing battles, so they become a big chore.

In addition to that, the battles take waaaaaaaaay toooooooooooo looooooooong, partly due to the ring puzzle at the start of every battle, and partly due to there just being too many enemies on the field for every battle.

I’m about 75% through this game, and I’m trying to decide if I want to continue, which sucks because I usually LOVE these games.

Just be careful with this one. You might want to watch some YouTube videos of it before you decide to commit to it or not.

I've been looking for a Bejeweled-like game for DS, so I've been trying those recommended to others who've asked this same question.

7 Wonders is the closest by far (Jewel Quest and Puzzle League are not).

Succeeding screens are not square, so you have to think more to remove jewels (called "runes" in this game) around the cut-out areas. Music is ok. Hints are given (little sparkles where a play is possible, but these are quite small on the ds).

There are "fireballs" and such, and they shoot out a horizontal row; another one takes out the vertical and horizontal row. There are "capstones" and "cornerstones" that appear, and you have to remove the runes below them so they fall out the bottom of the screen. These appear at random; it's not as though you have them to start out with and can plan strategy from the beginning of play. You get another life when you complete building what is at the level.

I haven't figured out why I get "hurry up" on the timing since I'm working quickly and very seldom have to spend time relying on a hint.

I haven't figured out whether there's an un-timed option. Does anyone know?

On my first cruise with it, I got up to the middle of the 3rd level. By that time, my eyes were bleary because of the size of the runes.

There's a little side story about guys building whatever it is and carrying picket signs when you don't get matches made quickly enough. There's a "conveyer belt" on the R side of the screen. As far as I can figure out, these are just for jollies.

Pros: (1) This has far fewer "auto-removes" and is more like Bejewled in this regard. (As opposed to Jewel Quest.) (2) Pleasing "clicking" sound as runes drop. (3) It's a stylus game. (4) Music is not horrible.

Cons: (1) It's timed. There may be a way to turn off the timed feature, but I don't know. Hope there is. I'd rather play until I get bored, rather than "die" and "get lives." (2) The jewels ("runes" in this game) are microscopic on the ds. I'm talking 2 mm. Quite a surprise if you've played the "real sized" one on your PC. (3) Also, it's difficult to tell pink and orange apart. (4) You can't save at the point where you failed. You have to go back to the beginning. (At this rate, I'll never even SEE what the art on the last level looks like!) Work-around: hit "start" and close unit. Keep it on the charger.

I bought my copy used at a local store ($18). The guy there said it had been discontinued but didn't know if that was because they were bringing out 2.0 or not. (I don't know whether he knew was he was talking about or not.)

UPDATE (11-08): I'm glad I got 7 Wonders and and reach for it most often (even before Touchmaster and Clubhouse Games!).

Final Fantasy 7, is one of those games that deals with a variety of aspects, instead of just focusing on one. It may seem to have just your simple everyday theme, of an average game. Once you get to actually playing the game, and beating it, you will understand what the whole concept of this game is about. It is more than just a battle of good and evil... it deals with what certain characters are going through at a time of crisis...
Story
The story in FF7 was very well done; fit very nicely with the characters and surroundings. At first playing FF7, I didn't really think much of the story... until they started to developing the characters, and other minor aspects in to place. Once the game progressed, I could tell that I was starting to become entwined with this game; not only physically, but emotionally as well. One thing on the story I feel that they could have portrayed better, would have been how it all started... they never really went into much depth of how it all started.
10/10
Appearance
At first glance at FF7, it doesn't really look like much. Basically looks like your "average" game, where you fight the bad guy, save the girl, and so on. The appearance of the game, also relies on the story. You have to understand what is going on, to get the whole meaning out of a certain scene. FF7, is one of those games that illustrates this property very well. At the time of the games release, which you can see here, it had some of the best graphics for any PSX game.
9/10
Characters
The characters of FF7 were portrayed beautifully. Another reason why FF7 had a unique character design, is because the characters had been introduced with some background information; instead of the traditional way, were they just introduce a character and that's that. The way that characters developed, in the game, also had its strong points to back up many of the games likings. The way that I first saw the game, character wise, was that each really didn't care about each other. Once the story, and overall plot thickened, the characters attitudes towards each other became more appealing.
9/10
Music
The music in the game was also another high end of the game. In my opinion, the music of the game, is what gave it that certain vibe, to make it a higher end game. I can't really say much about the music, though it was excellent. Overall Nobuo Uematsu did a very good at composing and producing the music of FF7.
9/10
Overall
Final Fantasy 7, what more can I say... This is one excellent RPG that I would recommend to anyone who is remotely interested in gaming. The overall atmosphere that Final Fantasy 7 brings with it, is incredible. The overall mixture of what it represents, varies from person to person. Some people call this "The greatest game of all time." and I fully agree with this statement... Gaming just doesn't get any better than this.
9.5/10...

Original review:
So far I've played the game for about 8 hours total and have been partnering up with my brother. So far, we've had no problems grouping up so that was a huge plus. Although, I should point out that my brother had issues one game getting everything to load. However, his problem was resolved after a restart. Furthermore, lots of people are drawing comparisons to Destiny. Yes, overall the game mechanic is quite similar. However, in my opinion Destiny was a huge disappointment for numerous reasons. While The Division isn't perfect, I'm enjoying it far more.

Pros:
-No crashes so far
-Great graphics
-Nice combination of an RPG and a shooter.
-Seems to have just the right amount of weapon and gear customization. Not too little and not too much.
-Interesting abilities so far from healing abilities to putting down turrets. And each ability can be modded.
-Matchmaking seems to have no issues so far. We've played a few matches with other players and haven't had any connection issues.
-Unlike Destiny, the story in The Division is clear and it honestly makes you feel like you're a part of something.
-Lots of missions to choose from and lots to do outside of combat...unlike Destiny

Cons
-Missions sometimes become active simply by walking too close to the mission start area even though you're traveling to another destination.
-As with any game, there have been a few random glitches. For example, we had one case where we jumped over all wall onto a train. But for some reason we couldn't jump down from the top of the train. So, we had to fast travel to a safe house.
-I can kind of see how after a while this game may start feeling repetitive. Some missions/encounters are quite similar. And after you reach level 30...about all you can do is replay old missions or go to the Dark Zone.
-Particularly when you first start the game or fast travel, be prepared for considerable load times.
-Not much incentive for constructing your own items. For example, at about level 30 you can build a Damascus sidearm which is suppose to be a high end gun. Well, shortly after building it (which took some time collecting the necessary components)....I found another sidearm that was actually better. And generally speaking as I was leveling up, just about every item I could make was no where near as good as what I already had equipped.

UPDATE:
Well, after being level 30 for a while and spending more time in the Dark Zone (I'm now DZ rank 50)...I'm going to have to give this game only 3 out of 5 stars. Seems every time we go up against someone else killing other players, they are IMPOSSIBLE to kill. In one case, we had ONE player destroy our entire team of 4. It was as if he was invincible. So I don't know if this is a matchmaking issue or what, but after having experienced this issue with the PvP almost every time we've gone out to the Dark Zone...its somewhat difficult for me to give this game a strong recommendation particularly when you get past level 30. Its not that difficult to ask for a BALANCED game where you actually have a chance in beating other players in PvP combat.

When I buy a game like this, I expect a good single player campaign along with a multiplayer component that will keep me hooked for quite a while. The Last of Us was a good example of a game that I felt did both really well. I've been a big fan since Uncharted 2...but this game ultimately is a let down for me overall. Don't get me wrong, although short...I found the single player enjoyable. But my 3 star rating was primarily to blame based on the disappointing multiplayer. I was expecting something as enjoyable as the last two titles. But the multiplayer so far in Uncharted 4 has been rather bland in my opinion after several hours of game play. When entering a match, you choose a loadout. That load out consists of a long gun, a pistol, and gear/boosters. You also have the option of a sidekick and what are called mysticals. On paper the sidekicks and mysticals sound cool/creative, but ultimately I think it still falls flat. Its simply nothing you're going to be amazed over, its just more of the same. And ultimately, just about everything Uncharted 4 does in the multiplayer, has already been done...numerous times. I'm also entirely disappointed there's no co-op arena or campaign.

So to sum up, if you want this game to simply finish up the story line, this is a good buy for you. If you're expecting a game that is coupled with an awesome multiplayer component...you'll probably be left disappointed.

Its sad some people are so blindly loyal to a game franchise like this one, they refuse to accept reality. And the reality is that the multiplayer in this game is a huge let down. Mortal Kombat 9 is generally touted as the greatest entry in the fabled fighting game series. The game brought the series back to its roots, returning to a 2D plane for fighting and bringing up all of the fan favorites from the first 3 games. All of these changes revitalized the franchise, bringing it back to its glory days of success, much different than the direction some of the 3D era titles were taking the franchise in.

So, when it was announced that a sequel was going to come out, fan expectations were high. Mortal Kombat X did a good job of meeting most of those expectations upon its initial release, but the XL version definitely cemented the game as a truly epic fighting game worth checking out. Mortal Kombat X introduced a new story mode that focuses on the Special Forces operatives, with the focal point being the newly created Cage family that consists of Johnny, Sonya and Cassie and their battle with Shinnok and efforts to save many of their friends lost in the previous game.

The game introduces a bunch of new fighters, ranging from children/relatives of established characters such as: Kung Jin, Cassie Cage, Jacqui Briggs, and Takeda, while also introducing new characters that fit in with more of the unusual non-human fighters such as: D'Vorah, Ferra-Torr, Kotal Kahn, etc. The children of the established characters (often referred to as the Kombat Kids) often feel forced down the throats of the players, as they are the upmost central point of the game's story mode. However, this is forgiven due to the high quality of gameplay the game offers.

MK X (and XL) plays at an incredibly fast pace, much faster than MK9 did, making it very easy to string together large combos that rack up damage as almost any character. This can make it difficult for newcomers to approach as they may find themselves losing more often during their early playing hours of the game. However, as they practice the game more, they will discover just how intuitive the gameplay is and how easy combo stringing is.

The XL version of the game comes with pretty much every single piece of DLC already loaded onto the disc. So, characters such as: Jason, Leatherface, Triborg (Cyrax, Sektor, Smoke and Cyber-Sub), Bo'Rai'Cho, Tanya, Goro, can all be played immediately. Most of the costume packs are already downloaded onto the disc, so costumes for fan favorite characters such as Scorpion, Sub Zero, etc will be readily available to use. The XL version also adds stage fatalities, something missing from the base game.

The online features work great, and the implementation of Faction Wars makes it so you have to select a Faction to side with, and depending upon how members of your faction perform in online fights you may earn rewards. Each faction also gives the players new fatalities specific to the faction they joined, these are called "Faction Kills".

Overall, the game is smooth, fast-paced, easy to learn, and diverse. The roster may not feature everyone from MK9, but most of the fan favorites are present: Mileena, Kitana, Reptile, Ermac, Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Kenshi, Sektor, Cyrax, Smoke, Liu Kang, Kung Lao, Quan Chi, Jax, Sonya, Kano, etc. There are some missing fan favorites like Noob Saibot and Baraka and Rain, and the story mode is definitely one of the weakest stories in MK history as it focuses too much on the new Special Forces units and the Kombat Kids. However, given that the only major negatives about the game stems from the story mode and not the gameplay, the mechanics or the content included with the game, it is easy to forgive these issues and at the current price that this game can be found for, it is an easy recommendation to make for fans of the series.

The Thrustmaster Ace Combat 7 Flight stick is a joystick and thrust assembly controller, designed for the PS4. As the name suggests, it works with Ace Combat 7 but it does also work with a small handful of other games including Elite Dangerous.

You can either operate the flight stick as a one piece stuck together combination, or with the aid of a small allen key which is included, separate out the thrust assembly from the joystick and have them separate. You get around a foot worth's of separation between the two but it does feel more natural than being squished together.

There are multiple buttons on both the joystick and thrust assembly which maps to all the buttons on the your standard PS4 controller as well as additional buttons for turning PS4 mode on and off. Why would you want to do this? Because this is a dual controller that works perfectly well on a PC as well. Just download the PC drivers from the Thrustmaster site, plug it in to a spare USB port and off you go. I've tried this combination on the PC with games like Combat Flight Sim 3 and Flight Simulator X and it works perfectly well.

The base of each controller is nice and sturdy with some heft to it so it stays in place on your desk/table when you are flying around. The joystick itself is also quite hefty but ergonomically contours very well to your hand and feels natural. The Hat is easily reachable with your thumb as are the trigger and buttons. As well as your normal directions of travel, the joystick also twists left and right which you can use as a rudder controller. It takes a little getting used to but after a while you don't even think about it, it comes naturally. There is a screw on the bottom of the joystick to make movement tighter or looser depending on your personal preference.

The thrust assembly is also meaty and is perhaps made for larger hands. Reaching the buttons can be a little bit of a stretch of your fingers/thumb but not too much. Also on the front of the thrust assembly is a rocker that is another rudder control if you don't like twisting the joystick. Personally I prefer twisting the joystick for use of the rudder rather than the rocker on the thrust assembly but it is nice that Thrustmaster have given you options.

Talking about rudder options, you can also buy separately rudder pedals that plug into this control set to operate with your feet if you want that more realistic feel.

This flight stick makes playing Ace Combat much easier and more realistic in my opinion. But as well as that, plug it into your PC and utilize it against any PC flight simulator. It is much better than using a controller and will improve your experience tremendously.

The only downside is the lack of compatible PS4 games although now that this exists perhaps that will grow over time. It is a little expensive if all you are going to do is play Ace Combat on the PS4 however if you plan on using it in conjunction with your PC as well then its not so bad.

Overall a great addition to the PS4 and Ace Combat game.

This is the new Oculus Quest 2, which is basically exactly the same as the older Quest except that it comes with half the memory, 128Gb of inbuilt storage rather than 256Gb and is priced $100 cheaper than the 256Gb version.

The Quest 2 is the perfect entry level headset to find out whether or not you like the VR world. Some people don't like VR for various reasons including vertigo and the feeling of getting sick, neck pain as the headsets are fairly heavy on your head etc. Other people love it and spend hours on it.

For your money your will get the headset itself, a fairly comfortable elastic strap to attach it to your head, two controllers and a charging cable. Setup is fairly simple. You connect it to your phone using bluetooth and just follow the prompts. You will need a Facebook account to tie it to and this puts some people off (I understand why) but the majority of people already have a facebook account anyway.

The Quest 2 has 2 1832x1920 LCD screens. Not quite 4K but a higher resolution than HD. For the money this isn't bad, especially considering the higher resolution Rift S is double the price. The eye pieces are slightly adjustable to 3 different positions, dependent upon the size of your head and space between your eyes. One great thing about the LCD display is that you can adjust the frame rate. I have mine set to 72Hz which I feel is much smoother than default 60Hz setting and this makes me much less prone to feeling sick. There is also a 90Hz refresh rate however for PC gaming that is too high unless you have a seriously beefy graphics card. Note however that you do not need a PC to use this.

The headset also has 3D capable audio built directly into the headset. The sound quality is OK but nothing outstanding. As such a lot of people also wear headphones when using the Quest 2 and there is a built in 3.5mm audio port to hook your headphones into. Personally, the sound is good enough for me and I prefer using it without the added weight of a pair of headphones.

The headset is quite heavy and although the soft elastic strap that comes with it is adequate, I would highly recommend purchasing one of the Elite, hard backed straps that you can find on amazon. These do make a lot of difference in distributing the weight, making wearing the headset much more comfortable and you can wear it for longer.

The Quest 2 has hundreds of apps and games available for it, from watching netflix and shooting games to fitness and boxing games. Even games such as boxing do help you to get in shape as you quickly find yourself ducking and weaving as well as throwing punches as you get immersed in the gameplay. These games are stored in the 128Gb of memory in the headset and aren't that large so even with 128Gb you should have plenty of room for a number of games and apps.

You can also attach your headset to your PC and play VR games on your PC. To do this you will need to buy an Oculus cable. The official one comes in at $80 which is very pricey. You can find third party cables that do the exact same thing for much less. I love to play DCS and Flight Simulator 2020 on my PC with the Quest. The immersion takes it to a whole other level, however in order to do so you will also need a fairly beefy PC to handle the graphics. My PC is a couple of years old, so its not powerful enough to turn up all the textures in Flight Sim to Ultra, but it is good enough to play with reasonably high definition. Honestly this is the main use I have for the Quest 2. At somepoint I will probably upgrade to the Rift S, but a new PC is in order before that.

So if your interested in dabbling with VR or don't have the budget to buy the Rift S then I would highly recommend the Quest 2. This 128Gb version, coming in at just $300 is well worth the money and I very highly recommend it.

This company, EA Sports has done it again. Their games can't be beaten, let's face it. Their latest release, Fight Night: Round 2 is the GREATEST Boxing game EVER! When I heard about another boxing game to be released by EA Sports, I rented the game as soon as it was released and as soon as I returned the rental, I was at Walmart next door purchasing my own copy. I just had to have this game. This game has it all! I can't imagine a better boxing game than this right here!

There is an excellent selection of gameplay options in this game. First, you can have a regular exhibition bout with any boxer from Featherweight - Heavyweight. The second option is CAREER mode. You can either use a boxer already in the game or CREATE a Boxer. The Create-A-Boxer mode is FANTASTIC. You build your fight from ground up. Everything from height, weight, body size, head size, face shape, different hair styles and colors, gloves, trunks, shoes, tattoos, taunts and Special punches. In this mode, if you have created a boxer, and choose to fight as him, before the fight, You will be required to participate in Fight Preparation. This is your opportunity to increase your boxer's stats before the fight. There are three training methods to choose from. One, "Combo Dummy" which works on Agility, Speed, Cuts and Heart. Two, is the "Heavy Bag." This works on Power, Speed, Stamina, Body, Chin, Cuts and Heart. Third is the "Weight Lifting." This works on Power, Stamina, Body, and Cuts. These training methods are fun. The mode "Hard Hits" is a typical exhibition but with different rules. After a knockdown the round is over. And there is no time limit to the rounds. Keep going until your opponent doesn't get up.

The career mode is fantastic. First, your fighter starts as a Amateur and you compete in ten fights until you become the Amateur champion and move on to Heavyweight. Now you will start out as the Number 50 contender and work your way up the ranks challenging opponents and earning money for every victory. The higher your fighter's rank, the more money each fight is worth. When you earn money, you can purchase more trunks, shoes, gloves, tattoos, punches, taunts, mouthguards, etc. There is a selection of over 100 different trunks.

The new features of the game are the EA Sports Cutman and the Total Punch Haymaker control. First, the EA Sports Cutman allows you to cure swelling and cuts between rounds your fighter has sustained during each round. THIS IS IMPORTANT TO LEARN! Why? If your fighter gets beaten enough and his face looks really torn up, the Referee may stop the fight. Second, is the EA Sports Total Punch Control Haymaker. Using the C-Stick on the controller, you can control the amount of power your fighter throws in his punches. You can use a Haymaker Hook, Uppercut, Body Uppercut and Hook using either arm. These blows will cut your opponent's face. If you time these punches just right, you can start a Flurry of haymakers right-left-right until your opponent collapses. Tip: IF YOU MISS, YOUR OPPONENT WILL TAKE ADVANTAGE WHILE YOUR FIGHTER IS VULNERABLE AND THROW STRONG PUNCHES AT YOU AND YOU MAY BE IN TROUBLE!

The graphics of this game are absolutely terrific. Very realistic. Your fighter's face will start swelling and bleeding accordingly as a fighter's would in real life. For instance, your fighter's eye won't swollen shut after 5 strong punches. Little by little the eye will get red, then a little bump under the eye, and gradually your fighter will look like he just went through a car wreck if he gets beaten enough. It is nice when your opponent has a shut eye cus of the swelling. It will effect his fighting and it will be easy to throw haymakers and knock him out. This game couldn't be any closer to real life than it already is. The body graphics are very detailed as well.

I LOVE THIS GAME! I am addicted to it. There could never be a better boxing game than EA Sports latest release, "Fight Night: Round 2." A quick tip, be patient, it takes a while to learn your way around the game and how to fight effectively. I give this game a 10/10 hands down. YOU DON'T EVEN HAVE TO BOTHER RENTING THE GAME FIRST! I Guarantee! Once you buy this game, you will never look back!

For 3 years, I had completed 6.5 seasons using MLB07. I didn't want to get the new version because I built such a foundation with the 2007 version but after 6 seasons, the rosters were WAY out of whack and too many computer created players on MLB rosters with the same faces!

This new version has its ups and downs. First, the graphics are poorer than MLB07. For example, Mark Teixeira is as white as a ghost. The fieling is a bit better. One plus side is the reality of the game. On MLB07, I was playing using "Hall of Fame" difficulty. In this version, I'm using "Veteran" and am facing a bigger challenge than 07's top level offered. I actually have tough down-to-the-wire games, even with the best of rosters. From that standpoint, it is more realistic with player stats and standings. In MLB07, all of my players batted .300+ and 7 of my 9 batters had over 100 RBIs. In this game, the numbers are more realistic as players hit hold/cold streaks like real life. Pitching is more realistic as well. Just as in real life pitchers have excellent, good and poor days.

One downside is the batting mode. I've adjusted the hell out of the batting sliders. In 07, I didn't have to adjust anything. In this version, for a player who in real life is MVP quality you have to increase the sliders when batting in order to get some real contact hits. Plus, if you call the right pitch and location, let's say it's going to be a fastball Low-Inside corner, the PCI will be stuck on middle-inside. Where to go from there is still tough to figure out. Whether or not to use the L stick a lot or just a little is a mystery still. It seems that if the PCI is an inch or two above the ball dot, just slightly move the L stick down, but the PCI doesn't move. Need to guess what part of the plate your batter is covering. After 3 months of a season, I'm just starting to get the hang of it.

So, if you want a more realistic game that will provide a bigger challenge, this is it.

I think maybe, just maybe, you have to play one or the other of JADE EMPIRE or KNIGHTS OF THE OLD REPUBLIC, but not both.

I've played both to completion, and really the difference seems to come down to this. The graphics and in-game fighting are significantly better in JE, but KOTOR gets the nod for better story line, acting and sound engineering.

Otherwise they're essentially very similar games. Aside from the fighting aspects(which in JE is real time, but in KOTOR is turn-based) and the specifics of the level-up process, the essential nature of the game is almost exactly the same. You encounter people, choose to help them or not, choose to respond to them in one way or another, and then your character is gradually pulled toward the "good" or the "bad" side of the spectrum. Bioware makes a claim that the choices you face are more varied here than they are in KOTOR--that there are more shades of "grey" in your possible responses--but I don't see any real evidence of that. It's more like this: in any field of possible answers there are three "obvious" choices (a "good" one, a "bad" one and a "neutral" one), then there are two "funny" ones (one one that leans toward "bad" and one that leans toward "good"). It's not like you have to really puzzle it out. But you DO have more to read.

What's interesting about this is, as the second DVD in this Limited Edition will make clear, the guys at Bioware did a lot of independent research to imbue the settings and story with "originality". Of course, since they were swimming in the same philosophical waters that Lucas enjoyed during his original conception of STAR WARS, they came to a lot of the same conclusions about the nature of good and evil, so, in the end, the commonalities between the two universes are more obvious than the differences.

This isn't to say that JADE EMPIRE is a bad game. Far from it. But it's hard to separate the two since both came from the same company, and since Bioware refused to make KOTOR 2 because they wanted to do something "original". The truth is that, though it's good, it's not very original. It's really is KOTOR by another name.

That's not an insult. To equal, and in some respects even exceed, KOTOR is no mere feat. For that reason, I can definitely recommend JE--but only to those who've never experienced KOTOR. I think those who are really familiar with KOTOR might want to rent this game to see how Bioware has continued to develop their craft, but its similarity to their earlier work are too obvious to make this an original entertainment in its own right. I see JE as a step in the natural evolution of console-based RPGs. I hope that now that they've proven it possible to combine real-time fighting with more traditional aspects of RPG storytelling and character advancement, we'll now see other games with this kind of "engine" applied to more original story lines.

[For those who have already decided to purchase the game, you might be wondering whether the Limited Edition is worth the price. And I would say yes. The "making of" material is definitely interesting, as is the playable demo. Most of it is not exclusive material. If you have G4 TV, you might have already seen these documentaries. But they are an interesting enough glimpse into the game creators' craft.]

I am 44 years old and find this game very addictive. I love the graphics style and universe of the dragon quest games so this game really peaked my curiosity. This game has a lot of similarities to the Minecraft games where building is concerned but that's where it  stops, and becomes its own very awesomely unique game. The games graphics are awesome, the characters aren't  made out of blocks with square bodies and heads which is something that annoys me about Minecraft. the awesome part is I start out by creating my own character, this includes gender, skin color, eye color, hair color, so you can customize your character to have your features, and make it your own however you like. Where this game shines the most aside from the awesome building aspect of it is the quests, they are fun, and not bland like Minecraft, and yeah they start out simple like collecting crafting items, building rooms, fighting off enemy hordes, and meeting new friends. And I love love love that you can make weapons, tools, shields and armor for your character so that he can become more powerful against any enemy he/she comes across. Fighting is also fun in the game because there is a little strategy to it not just hack slash, also your character does learn new moves like a spin attack that looks like Link's spin attack from Legend of Zelda games which I think is really awesome. Also you can craft tons of health items to take with you in case you get low fighting beasts out in the big world. The makers of this game put a lot of thought into it, and made it into a much funner more unique game that clearly overshadows Minecraft games in my opinion. Never have I been so absolutely torn between loving and hating a game as with The Surge.

Just, finally, beat it last night (and immediately started NewGame+...that should show you how much I actually like the game) after 40 hours of dying, dying, dying some more, dying, grinding, dying...etc.

Seriously - this game is brutal. Maybe I'm just not good at these games - probably, since I own Demon's Souls, every Dark Soul's game, etc., and have never played them. You will die a lot; an enemy which you killed easily will completely destroy you the next time you run past it. A boss which you easily dodged a hundred time (before then being one-hit killed when it was almost dead) will one-hit-kill you out of the gate when you go back. Dropped your cash? No problem - run and get it, unless said boss one-hit kills you while you're going to pick it back up.

On that topic, you're going to lose a LOT of money because of BS deaths. The maps are also frustrating as hell - none are particularly big, there is no actual map, so you never know exactly were to go, or what to do, you're just constantly running around lost.

Now that I've beaten the game..all of these negatives? Not so much - I think that the developers are brilliant. That annoying boss fight? There is always more than one way to do it, and while you WILL die, you slowly figure out 'tricks' to beating them. The lack of a map? Well, in NewGame+, once you've grinded through every level the first time, you know where to go in the levels, and can constantly find new areas that you missed. And the design? It's brilliant - everything links back in on itself; it's actually impressive how they were able to do that. There is a bunch of gear, lots of weapons...

Wow, what a great idea for a game. Take the classic descent into Hell, ripped from the pages of medeival poet Dante Alighieri's "The Divine Comedy," but just make it all a little more kickass -- for example, instead of Dante the poet as the protagonist, let's make Dante a scythe-wielding crusader with a cross stitched into his bare chest. And do it in the style of the classic action franchise "God of War." Yeah, that's what I'm talkin' 'bout right there! What a concept!

Well, I'd be lying if I said this game wasn't fraught with missed opportunities. But not nearly as many as you've probably heard. Critics were unduly harsh back in early 2010 when "Dante's Inferno" streeted, perhaps because it is undeniably a "God of War" clone and perhaps because the game does admittedly lose some steam near its conclusion. But as for me, I had more fun slashing my way through Hell than I've had in quite some time. Gamespot's score of a 6.5 out of 10, for example, certainly doesn't do this game justice. "Dante's Inferno" may not deliver on all of its many promises, but it comes damn close.

Again, you are cast as Dante, but not the Dante we know from history. This Dante is a deeply flawed individual who manages to earn your affections merely because of his stubborn refusal to accept his fate, or that of his lover Beatrice whose soul is condemned to Hell for having a little too much faith in his virtue. He's a dark, brooding character in much the same vein as Kratos from "God of War" (which is undoubtedly not a coincidence). And like Kratos, he's a real badass. At the beginning of the game rather than die from a should-be fatal wound, he hands the Grim Reaper his ass and steals Death's own scythe, claiming it as his own before heading south toward Hell in an attempt to redeem himself and rescue his beloved Beatrice from the affections of a very horny Lucifer. It's dark but overblown enough to still feel like a video game story instead of a somber meditation on the afterlife. In fact, peeling back the onion that is Dante's character makes for a very compelling story, and the title character is certainly one of the deeper and more interesting video game characters to come along in quite some time -- this side of the Ghost of Sparta, anyway.

It's satisfying as Hell (pun intended) to kill waves upon waves of demons with Dante's stolen scythe. But as scary as that weapon looks, it's Beatrice's crucifix (which literally shoots crosses into his demonic enemies' faces) that really gets the job done. In fact, that cross must be twice-blessed by Jesus Christ Himself, because its mere presence greatly reduces much of the game's challenge factor on lower difficulty settings, as it's a powerful ranged attack that can never be depleted. Combining this with the scythe, some very cool magical attacks, a quite fair number of combo moves, and, best of all, some tight controls makes killing things in this Hell seem like Heaven.

And the design of the game, by and large, is very inspired. Morbidly inspired, granted, but such is the source material. Sure there are a few typical horned demons to contend with as well as some flying creatures that could just about cameo in any action game ever made, but then there are the truly grotesque souls of Lust who, despite a very feminine appearance at first glance, are not shy about thrusting a huge, claw-tipped penis directly at your face. Likewise the mutant souls of Gluttony are gas-filled flesh bags who don't mind using vomit and/or shite as a weapon. Boss encounters are likewise quite memorable, including such baddies as one who rips swords from his own body and throws them at you and one which pits you against the eyeless guardian of the gates of Hell -- the decider, so to speak, of which souls belong in which circle of Hades. It's unfortunate that Lucifer, "Big D" himself, in all three of his guises no less, comes off as just plain silly. First he's a groping shadow-man, then he's a giant laughable beast with bat wings for a goatee, and finally he's your typical horned satyr whose only memorable trait is his giant swinging balls and a member that could make Mr. Ed jealous. After fighting a three-headed beast with mouths for eyes and a demonic Cleopatra with tongues for nipples, Lucifer himself just doesn't get the blood pumping.

But perhaps this boss encounter with the Devil himself best describes the "Dante's Inferno" experience. Early on, the game is amazing -- a true contender to the "God of War" throne with its epic story, cinema-quality production values, and of course its depiction of Hell. Again, you've barely been playing the game for five minutes when you challenge the Grim Reaper himself to a duel. Now that's how you kick off an action game! And despite what you've probably read, the game stays strong up until maybe the 80% completed point. After the tangled forest of Suicide, it's admittedly all downhill, but just getting to this point -- what a ride it's already been.

Unfortunately that's when the real suffering begins, as the devs clearly tried to pad out a somewhat short experience by scrapping solid level design and forcing you into a series of trials that would be better suited as bonus content. For example, you are tasked with killing a series of respawning enemies without using magic at one point, and then killing five creatures while attacking from the air without ever letting them touch the ground. It's silly, it's boring, and it feels like exactly what it is -- padding. Many reviews have mentioned this portion of the game as something of a deal-breaker, but I argue is it any worse than the final portion of "Devil May Cry 3" that forced you (again bearing the name Dante) to repeat several previous boss encounters before you could proceed to the endgame? And that game was quite acclaimed when it came out despite an equally, if not far more annoying buildup to the final confrontation. Those bosses were hard as hell to beat the first time -- fighting them again was just plain infuriating.

All this leads to the aforementioned final battle with the Devil himself, which again fails to fire on all cylinders, but the same is true of many good games. One just wishes "Inferno" didn't feel like two development teams worked on the damn thing -- one, creating 80% of the game, doing a "God of War" worthy job, while the other, responsible for that last 20% not really having much of a clue what makes a good hack-and-slash actioner work. It's this split personality that sadly prevents me from hailing "Dante's Inferno" as a modern classic, but it still comes dangerously close. The music, the voice acting (apart from a silly-sounding Lucifer), the story, the atmosphere, the cinemas, and the gameplay are all excellent. Perhaps the only other flaw that bears mentioning is the annoying 40 second long minigame one must slog through to save the tortured souls of Hell -- it makes the notion of damning them instead and salvaging those 40 seconds of your life, even if you want to redeem Dante's own tortured soul, far too tempting indeed. But virtually everything else in "Dante's Inferno" achieves A-list status, and were it not for such an epic fumble near the finale, what a ride this would be. Hell, even opening doors is fun -- you impale a fat demon with your scythe and pound a button until the stubborn S.O.B. rolls up like an iron curtain and gives you access to the next chamber. Good stuff.

So yeah, it's true that this game has some very tragic flaws. But if you're a fan of hack-and-slash action games like "God of War" or even "Devil May Cry," miss Dante's descent into woe at your own peril. This is very nearly a classic, but, as per usual, the Devil had to go and screw it up.

Final Score: 8.0

Dinner last night may have been great, but it's not so great when you heat up the leftovers for supper the next evening. Maybe it's soggy now. Or lukewarm. It just doesn't taste the same, despite consisting of all the same ingredients. Which brings me to "Bioshock 2." I loved the original. It was one of the greatest, most original and atmospheric games ever released. It may have been the spiritual successor of the equally amazing "System Shock" series, but it was entirely its own thing. As for its sequel, well... I liked Neil Marshall's horror flick "Descent" too, but that didn't mean they should have made "Descent Part II," a pointless, unoriginal retread that had very little new to offer, and what was new wasn't very good and reflected negatively on the original. I feel exactly the same way about "Bioshock 2."

I never saw the need for a sequel to begin with, in all honesty, as the first "Bioshock" wrapped itself up quite well. Now, "Bioshock Infinite" is in the works, almost acknowledging that a straight "Bioshock" sequel was always a bad idea in much the same way as the "Prince of Persia" franchise decided to go back to what worked with "The Forgotten Sands" after that next-gen reboot that might as well have played itself. Granted, "Infinite" is trading an underwater city for a flying city (very imaginative), but it's DIFFERENT. It has the potential to do what "Bioshock" did the first time around -- take what we love about that game but make it fresh again. Basically, everything that, I feel, "Bioshock 2" failed to do.

In "Bioshock 2," you get to play as a Big Daddy out to rescue his abducted Little Sister, and that's about as far as the game goes toward forging its own identity. You still tool around in Rapture, which looks almost exactly the same as it did when you last left it. You still scavange everything you can find while squaring off with those Adam-addicted freaks. The gameplay is identical in almost every way, but with one difference -- we've already done this, and there's no compelling reason to do it again when you could just as easily pop your far superior copy of the original "Bioshock" in and give it another playthrough. Even the game's most tauted feature, playing as a Big Daddy, is weakly executed. You feel every bit as fragile as you did in the first game, and aside from your armored hands filling the screen, it's hard to tell you're not the same protagonist from game one except for the fact that you can now march around with a Little Sister riding on your shoulder and directing you toward the next source of Adam.

I think critics put on the kiddie gloves when this game stepped into the ring earlier this year. My admiration for the first "Bioshock" doesn't cloud my judgment though when it concerns the sequel -- in fact, quite the opposite. The overwhelming feeling of sameness just kept creeping in on me during my time with "Bioshock 2," like I'd done all of this before only better. The first game's story was far superior on top of it -- especially the "Would you kindly?" revelation near the end, perhaps gaming's best ever "Gotcha!" moment. There are no such moments here, although the chance to see things from an entirely different and very eerie perspective near the game's conclusion is certainly the best moment in "Bioshock 2." But it can't hold a candle to learning the truth about your supposed benefactor in the original game.

And that's the problem. There's just not enough that's new here, and what is new just can't compete with what came before. Even the whole playing as a Big Daddy angle, were it executed better, still wouldn't be all that fresh since something similar essentially happens at the end of the first game. Basically, there are two camps of people who "Bioshock 2" is for -- those who missed the first one (Why?!), and those who played the first one several times and still can't get their fill of Rapture. On those grounds, this glorified expansion pack is certainly worth its weight in gold. But if you loved the first game, and let's face it you probably did, but expected much more out of a proper sequel, you'll probably be just as disappointed by this return to Rapture as I was. This makes it a hard game for me to actually score, but let me put it this way -- I was playing this and "Metro 2033" at around the same time, and constantly found myself being wooed away to the mutant-haunted tunnels of Moscow and turning my back on the undersea mess that was Andrew Ryan's supposed utopia...
