The inevitability of having to move on from Tiger Woods after such a long relationship put EA Sports in a position where they felt it necessary to take the rebooted PGA Tour series in a totally different direction. Rory McIlroy PGA Tour has aimed at appealing to a more “casual” consumer. Gone are healthy lineups of licensed courses and golfers, and nods to history of the sport. In their place are arcade-elements like fantasy courses and over-the-top mini-games.

Over two years have passed since Tiger Woods PGA Tour 14, and the new McIlroy title comes up short compared to that game in most every area that matters.

As a product, Tiger 14 offered significantly more content, all of which was far more compelling than what’s found in McIlroy, which feels barren and dull in comparison. It’s a struggle to find things that McIlroy does better.

To its credit, the courses included in McIlroy look spectacular, and the presentation of them is fantastic. There’s some graphical blur and pop-in but otherwise the game looks nice despite appearing to be sub-1080p. The commentary is an improvement, though inaccurate at times, and the crowd sounds are decent though not always responsive at the right moments. The crowd looks good, is active, and you even see them applauding and walking around.

The Prologue, which is essentially a guided tour through big moments of the US Open by McIlroy, ends up being the most interesting aspect of the game and that’s over after 20 minutes. Features one would hope for and expect, like tiebreaker playoffs and replay functionality, are absent. Instead some questionable design decisions have been made.

Career Mode is very basic. There isn’t even a calendar you can view of upcoming events. Maybe that’s to hide that the lack of courses will make the mode stale fairly quickly. Adding in the “Quick Rounds” feature, which is defaulted on and already has people confused and wondering why they can only play a few holes each round, only compounds that concern.

There are merits in allowing people to play through rounds quicker and certainly many people will appreciate the ability to do so. However it really creates a detached feeling, only playing 4-5 holes per round, and the sense of potential accomplishment vanishes along with it. At least it’s only an option but EA should have given people the choice up-front, similar to what they’ve done with the “Gameplay Styles”, rather than making it the default way to play in Career.

Then there’s the pathetic create-a-golfer system. In a game that puts so much weight on playing with a created golfer, inherently due to the make-up of the game and the thin roster of licensed golfers, it’s really unacceptable. It’s also worth noting there is no “GameFace” type feature, which bizarrely was prioritized for NBA Live instead.

Rory McIlroy PGA Tour has only 8 licensed courses on disc, plus 4 fantasy courses. There are only 12 licensed golfers. This game offers less than half of what Tiger 14 had a launch as far as courses and golfers go.

One thing that works in McIlroy is the offering of three different “Gameplay Styles”. Other sports games would be wise to offer various ways to play that may be more accommodating to different people. The three offer different approaches that span from the “arcade” to the more “sim” – though the sim Tour style is still fairly easy to pick up and play. It seems that no matter how badly the shot stroke is mangled, the shot will go straight, it’s just a question of distance. Putting and getting out of precarious positions presents the extent of the challenge.

The lack of loading time between holes (which The Golf Club has too) was touted heavily in promotion. Undoubtedly it’s a benefit to the new game but loading times into the courses are lengthy, and menu navigation is unresponsive and frustratingly laggy.

I’m not against mini-games. I actually think they have a place within all sports games, even the sim-centric ones. They can be used as a teaching tool where people improve skills through the process that can then be applied to the actual games. The Night Club Challenge though is more of its own thing. It’s not going to help people in a way that translates to the normal golfing. It feels like something you’d play on your phone.

The Night Club Challenge has some appeal despite that and is mildly fun – some will probably find it to be more and that’s especially true of completionists and those who enjoy the challenge of topping previously held high scores. The mode is boring at first but after a few challenges it starts to become more interesting. That’s when boosts start getting introduced and even elements like portals make their way in. I’ve gone through 24 of the 62 on Wolf Creek so far and there are still Paracel Storm and Coyote Falls to unlock along the way.

EA decided to introduce a new element into Online Play by rendering the other players onto the course along with you. In theory it sounds interesting but in practice it’s a dismal failure. Those players appear out of thin air and then vanish. They’re nothing more than a distraction. It was actually better in the past when you’d see their shot arcs instead. Online matches also have no commentary or crowd noise, making it a completely empty experience and a bore to play. Potentially it could be better with groups of friends who are chatting on mic together but that’s the only scenario where it would be passable.

What EA Sports has delivered with Rory McIlroy PGA Tour is a game that doesn’t have enough content to justify its price at launch, and what it does have won’t resonate strongly with either the “sim” or “casual” crowd. EA has made mistakes with some other games in the past where they try and go this route of angling for ways to market a “sim” series to a “casual” audience. The results have been products that have no true identity, disappoint in sales, and are quickly forgotten. It would seem unlikely that McIlroy will avoid that same fate.

This is definitely a 3-star pad for most people, but if you have larger hands, this *may* be a 4-star product. The gist here is that its' fine, but has some issues and definitely not as good as the stock Dual Shock 4.

Hori makes good quality pads (this is erroneously credited to "Sony" here on Amazon, with the manufacturer's named mushed into the name of the controller in the title), but this isn't one of their better ones. Build-wise, its actually pretty solid, but feels lighter than it looks. The inputs seem like they'd be squishy, but surprisingly respond well while playing. The quality is pretty good, I'll be honest. The biggest problem with this is the actual molding. See how the top of this thing is kinda chunky? Kinda... squared off instead of being smooth and round? The way the handles are molded, they guide your fingers to rest on the R2 and L2 buttons and actually overshoot the L1/R1 buttons a bit. You're going to have to reach for them, even if its subtle and you don't notice at first, you might start cramping if you're hitting those buttons a lot. Or if you're like me, you just stop hitting those buttons as much. After using this for a few days now, its weird how issues pop up because of its mold & design, but they're there and you'll notice them after playing awhile. It's just not as comfy as the Dual Shock 4.

Being a Hori Product though, the instructions are in Japanese, so I had to figure out how to use the extra buttons on my own. Oh right, this controller has a few added buttons over a standard pad; a Turbo button (hold turbo down, then tap whatever other button you want to "turbo up"), an Assign button (see below: its complicated), an extra "Target" trigger on the inside of the left handle on the back for functions to be assigned to (see attached pic: where your pointer finger naturally wants to land when holding the controller without putting fingers on top), a PS4/PS3 toggle (I'm actually pretty sure the normal Dual Shock 4 will auto-detect if its connected to a PS3), and another mysterious toggle switch next to that on the underside. Its marked with a "dot dash line" graphic (see the attached pic), and I don't know what that does AT ALL. So have fun figuring out that mystery! In all honestly, none of these are super useful anyway. They're just, I don't know, non-issues.

>>>>>>> To use the Assign button
After tinkering with this for awhile, and getting frustrated, and screwing up the buttons, I finally bumbled my way into figuring this thing out. It is NOT intuitive. I would LOVE to know how the instructions describe this nonsense.

1. If you hold "Assign", the TURBO button's green LED will turn on.
2. Next, tap the button you want to program (I highly recommend JUST using the Target trigger; you can easily overwrite any other button's function though if you want to for some reason), The green LED under Turbo will start blinking; you can record a function now.
3. Hit another button, and the Assign button's red LED should now turn on. This means it has programmed the button in Step 2 to do the function of the button you hit here in Step 3.

IF you screw up, HOLD the Assign button and just... tap the button you you screwed a lot. As fast as you can. Do it until green Turbo LED starts blinking. Then it & the Assign buttons' red LED should turn off, or like turn on and then off. Anyway, once they're off, all button functions should return to normal. It is REALLY unintuitive.

>>>>>>>

Cramming these extra buttons and triggers onto the controller seems to have cramped up the face of the controller a bit as far as the touchpad and the Share/Options buttons are concerned. Not that you'll hit them reliably anyway, because they're practically sunk in. They're really, really flat on the face of the thing. They also changed the shape to simple little circles. If you like capturing/sharing videos and screenshots, do NOT buy this controller. The Touchpad feels just as good as the official one, and is just a little smaller and actually easier to hit accidentally (reaching for the Share button, for example), but its such a seldom-used feature in most PS4 games that I don't find that as a notable flaw.

So it's definitely not perfect. I like Hori, they make some great 3rd party controllers, and have ever since the Gamecube/PS2 era at least. I have a Fighting Stick Mini from them for my PS3/4 and I love it. I have an old SNES shaped Gamecube controller from them; also love it. This too is generally well MADE; it doesn't feel cheap. But its not particularly well-DESIGNED, and comes off as a disappointment from them. Its also weird that its so expensive (its practically the same price as the stock DS4), yet it isn't wireless. If you've got long fingers and/or big hands, go for it. You'll probably enjoy this, no problem. But if you're fine with the feel, size and dimensions of the official DS4, this is far away from that and could be a bit of a problem. Its probably worth a pass in that case.

Its absolutely not horrible, but it is clearly inferior to the Dual Shock 4 overall thanks to its form factor; its just too clunky/edgy and weird up top.

4 Goddesses Online is a real gem, and as I enjoy action games more than turn-based RPGs, is my personal favorite Neptunia game to date.

Its a great little parody/satire of that annoying "Isekai" anime trend that's going on right now (where a bland nerd gets thrown into a video game fantasy world and inexplicably becomes a hero), and that definitely deserves a proper send-up these days, so props for Neptunia for delivering one. Of course, these games are always funny and cute and 4GO is no exception. The important thing is that it's a good excuse for this series to switch gears from their other main RPG titles and spinoffs to instead deliver a *very familiar experience* to anyone who's played Phantasy Star Online, Ragnarok Odyssey ACE, God Eater Rage Burst or anything like that. And let me tell you, it's a pretty good imitation, y'all (^-^).

Combat is pretty straightforward - you have an attack button... that's it! It sounds too simple, but it's fast, responsive, flashy and satisfying with every character in the game, from the up close sword users like Nep to the distance fighting used by characters like the dual pistol-wielding thief, Uni. There may be only one button to hit, but it is fun to experiment with the different fighting styles the characters have. Thankfully the developers at Tamsoft have implemented a "Perfect Guard" that keeps the melee fighting WAY MORE ENGAGING than in their previous Neptunia game, Action Unleashed, and rewards you for getting familiar with the timing of enemy attacks. The Magic System is also pretty straightforward - just hold L1 and hit a face button, and switch between two palettes using up and down on the dpad - and reminiscent of how Dragon Quest Heroes 1 + 2 does it. It's all bolstered by a proper upgrade and leveling up system, as well as a proper questing system, with your item shops and weapon/armor upgrades and cosmetics... all that stuff. So there's plenty of stuff to improve and new gear to work towards. I'm telling you, somehow it's not as dumb and simplistic as it feels like it should be. Props to the developers, seriously.

It all runs in Unreal 4 now too, resulting in the nicest-looking game in the series by far with sharp, vibrant cel-shaded characters and some nice materials in the much larger levels now, but it's not a perfect transition to the modern era for the series. The biggest technical hang-ups I've encountered is the inexplicable load on startup every time (it's like 2 minutes or something) and the fact that large characters (just bosses, pretty much) can often get stuck in the ground collision, or worse, get YOU stuck if you're a melee class that is currently in their face engaging them. It takes quite a bit of squirming (jumping, running, hitting the dodge button, switching characters like a maniac - just whatever you can do) to get out of that when it happens, but it just never was a real problem for me, I dunno? It really forces you to get good at those perfect counters in a hurry though ;) There are also frame rate issues, and the game crashed on me twice (I never had my save corrupt, but it definitely is nice to have PS+ Cloud backups whenever you see that happen, eh? Just for peace of mind's sake). But it just never seemed like that big of a deal.

And that's really the case throughout. Like, there ARE issues here - they're obviously to see - but NONE of them got in the way of the enjoyment I'm having playing it. Even underneath the performance issues, anyone should be able to see there is obviously a solid action-RPG here with a killer, vibrant artstyle and cool characters. Having played through to the first ending so far, and gotten all 12 characters up to at least 70, I'm absolutely nowhere near bored of this. The game looks great, is a super fun action game (certainly the best game Tamsoft has ever developed), and somehow manages to avoid becoming as one-note or repetitive as it should be considering how simple the combat is on paper. Meanwhile, the story and writing & voiceover are as charming, cute and silly as these games always are. Heck, the soundtrack is even surprisingly good too. It's just a good time.

It's honestly probably a 4-star game (3.5 at the lowest) since it's got those problems I mentioned, but I gotta give it a 5-star because I'm enjoying it just so, so much. If you're sitting on the fence, maybe wait for a price drop - that's understandable. But in a year with a ton of amazing, but lengthy and serious RPGs/Adventures to go through (Persona 5, Tales of Berseria, NieR Automata, FFXV's myriad updates, etc. etc. etc.), this is a breath of fresh air. It's just another delightful Neptunia game, and a must-play for anyone who enjoys action-RPGs like this.

**Note about Online: I can't speak a whole lot on the multiplayer (my internet is not great most of the time), but it seems to work fine. There's a fully chat system with pre-existing phrases for you to use, and also free chat, and it can perform perfectly - I can vouch for that. I haven't had too much trouble looking for games either, but I haven't been looking too much either. Sometimes you find rooms, sometimes you don't, the one time I made one it got populated relatively fast I think (I multitask a lot though, so I don't really notice a long wait in a game when I got work to do on my PC right next to it). It's good; it should be totally functional and it seems like the community is pretty nice.

This is a great game--my new favorite. I have to give it 5 stars overall. The scenery is probably the best I've personally seen on the PS4. The weapons and equipment are pretty realistic, in my opinion. I just recently stopped playing Metal Gear Solid 5 after playing that and nothing else over the last 9 months. I believe this game is like Far Cry 4, GTA 5, MGS 5, and Fallout 4 all wrapped into one (with a little imagination). I own all those games for PS4, and I believe this game takes most of the best elements from the others mentioned above. The sheer number of vehicles and weapons and equipment is amazing. There are some significant pros and cons to this game, however. In no particular order, I don't agree with being able to switch to any weapons that have been unlocked whenever I feel like it. I'm not carrying all my unlocked weapons with me at all times--that would be extremely cumbersome. For the fun factor, tho, it is great. My favorite sniper so far is the MSR. I don't have the 50 cal unlocked yet, but I'm told it can even shoot down the Apache helicopter with 1 shot. My favorite machine gun is the M249. Nothing stands up to the 249 except the "Apache" Unidad helicopter, which incidentally looks almost exactly like a Cobra helicopter. I was carrying a bullpup assault rifle with a grenade launcher, but that pales in comparison now to the damage the trusty M249 deals out. I'm still using the standard 45 caliber pistol. I use everything suppressed except the 249. I absolutely HATE that (at least on Arcade level) I cannot drag off the bodies of enemies I've killed. I believe that should have been implemented into this game. I loved that on Far Cry 4. As for the Unidad, I think it's total BS that I can shoot down a gazillion Unidad helicopters, obliterate hordes of Unidad soldiers, and destroy lots and lots of Unidad vehicles, and they just keep coming and coming and coming--and then they kill me. I have pushed the Unidad alert level to LEVEL 4 on several occasions, just to see if I could kill them all. Even on Arcade level, I can't kill them all. Another thing that is hokey is a minivan should not be able to go up an almost vertical mountain. It is fun, tho. The vehicles take an extreme amount of damage before they blow up, generally. In real life (which I realize this is a game), I would not be able to take a Lambo-looking sports car cross-country and run over cactus after cactus and smash into stone walls, etc, etc, etc, without totaling the thing out in the first crash. I LOVE the sync-shots. It really helps with the stealthy sniper approach. When all else goes to hell, tho, I bring out the M249 and get to work. I really like being able to upgrade weapons, as with Fallout 4. I like stopping vehicles and pulling people out and taking their cars as with GTA5. The scenery really reminds me a lot of MGS5 and FC4. Not surpising, considering who produced this game. What I really, really, really like about this game is it IS fun. I have probably spent 30 hours playing so far, and it has gone by like a snap of my fingers (almost). And, I'm just on the very easiest level. I am going to have to get a lot better at this game to even think about upping the difficulty level. The AI on this game is really pretty good. My AI soldiers, as in my 3 teammates and the rebel soldiers, are really pretty good. They have senior moments on occasion and can't figure out where to go, but for the most part, they are right there beside me or at least very close in a gunfight. The enemy soldiers AI reminds me a lot of MGS5. One shot unsuppressed (and sometimes even suppressed), and they have my location, and they are coming for me and my team. I hate the SAM missle sites. I have gone in and wiped them out in order to steal an aircraft only to discover that there was another SAM missile launcher in range that enjoyed shooting me down. Flares would have been a nice touch to be able to drop out of an airplane or heli, I am going to try switching seats with another player and try decoying an incoming missile with a flare gun, but I bet it won't work. But I am going to try it if I can line everything up. I have gotten stuck in the map 3x so far. Each time, I have fallen down into a crevice somewhere, and the only way I could get out was to fast travel out. That used to happen to me in Skyrim back in the day. But for the miles and miles or km and km of map this game has, I suppose I can excuse a couple glitches here and there. I'm pretty sure this is operator error, but I am not good at base jumping yet. I've got it figured out how to jump out of a heli or an airplane, tho. The parachute is really cool. There are a ton of different vehicles available. I hardly have to walk anywhere, but I do it just to try to discover everything on the map. Usually everywhere I go there is lots of ammunition available, which is nice. Not sure how realistic that is, but it makes the game more fun. I don't like how I have to stand directly in front of the ammunition crates in order to re-load ammo. Same thing goes for the supply tagging. It seems like I have to be right in front and touching each crate in order to load or tag. When doing air-to-air combat, it is difficult for me to fly a heli and shoot the guns all at the same time while still trying not to get shot down. Luckily, my guys out on the sides of a small heli do a lot of shooting, and they take out a lot of enemies while I perform my "circle of death" going around and around a target. I'm sure some company will come up with a game better than this in the future, but for now, this game is the bomb. 5 stars.

*** UPDATE 4/3/17 ***

I still love this game. I'm level 28 now. I've unlocked a lot of cool weapons and gear. My favorite loadout is still the MSR in the sniper slot, M249 in the light machine gun slot, the P45T in the pistol slot, and the standard drone. For destroying vehicles and especially that pesky Unidad "Apache", I do switch to the HTI for a 1-shot kill. I have been using the explosive drone a lot for taking out SAM sites and generators. Some of the bases are almost impossible to get into, and the explosive drone really helps on occasion. For example, there is a Serpentidad (or something spelled close to that) in the bottom center of the map. It is crawling with Unidad. It also has a SAM site and a generator. Blowing up the generator opens all the gates, and destroying the SAM site helps with a mission underneath it on the map in order to steal a +3000 medical supplies helicopter. I had to attempt that mission 3 times to get it done. I got shot down 2x, and then I figured out that the SAM launcher was in that Unidad base. So, I had to take out the SAM site first in order to not get blasted out of the sky by missiles on the 3rd (and successful) attempt. So far, the SAM launchers and Unidad are my worst enemies. I can't say for sure how many, but I think I shot down about 15 Apache helicopters one time when I was discovered sneaking around the Unidad base after I had released all the prisoners out of the prison. It is ridiculous how many soldiers and land-based vehicles and helicopters spawn almost immediately after the previous units have been destroyed. They just keep coming and coming, in waves LOL, and the only way I have found so far to get the Unidad alert down from 4 stars is to run and hide somewhere that Unidad cannot find me. Eventually, they give up, but it takes a really long time to outrun Unidad. I have still been playing on the easiest level so far since beginning the game. I have discovered almost everything on the massive map, but I still have a long, long way to go before I can finish the game. I also think it is a bit unfair for me to spot and mark targets with my drone and my AI crew somehow targets them and can wipe them out with a single shot, sometimes even thru what appears to be solid walls. My recommendation is to get the MSR, HTI, M249, and the explosive drone as soon as possible. I also think that the fastest revive skills and best binocular skills are a must. The binoculars are very handy maxed out for when drones are jammed. I have now seen videos where the streamer uses the EMP drone almost exclusively to take down road convoys. I haven't done that yet. I usually just assault the escort vehicles from the air and then land next to the truck and loot it. From the ground, I usually shoot up the rear escort vehicle and then run the other 2 vehicles off the road and loot the truck. I love the helicopters for close air-to-ground combat. I fly, and the AI teammates shoot the crap out of everything once I give the order. I'm thinking I may start playing online, but I haven't done it yet. I'm thinking that human teammates will probably do better than the AI. BUT, the AI teammates are very good, in my opinion. The AI enemies are almost always very good. A couple times the AI teammates and the AI enemies have gotten stuck around vehicles or other obstacles, but usually they are very, very "smart", sometimes too smart, especially when I get surprised by an enemy AI it seems that way. I've gotten stuck in the map a couple more time and have had to fast travel out. Not a huge deal, but a minor irritation. Even when I happen to get KIA and re-spawn fairly close to the mission objective, I hardly ever do it the same way the second (or third) time around. It just seems like the AI soldiers surprise me sometimes by taking different routes, especially in the cities. At a fixed location, like a "steal an airplane" mission, they are pretty much in a concentrated area, but they do walk around a lot sometimes, and if they are alerted, they will come looking for me. I absolutely hate the "X" being the machine guns on my helicopters setup. The way I fly, I don't think I can (or will) change the button to control the fixed guns on helicopters. In order to shoot from anything other than head-on, I have to tip the nose of the heli way down in order to shoot down from any significant height to engage targets on the ground. I believe I have crashed my helis several times because I was pushing too many buttons and manipulating the joysticks on my PS4 controller all at once. I love (and hate) the bullet drop on the weapons. I don't think there is too much side wind pushing on the bullets, but there is definitely bullet drop for many calibers once I'm shooting over 200m. I like this so much better than Far Cry 4 in that respect. The game is still really fun for me, and I'm going to keep playing it until I'm tired of it. 5 stars remains!

I didn't go very far into the game, so I'll be brief.

Pros:
- Strong RPG elements. You get to choose the styles of an agent you want to be.
Story and Script is interesting. Skills and missions are plenty.

Con:
- I don't know about the console versions, but the PC version has this particular issue that made me uninstall this game.

EVERY TIME the game loads a new area or a new information (like an incoming radio contact or a new objective), the camera jerks out of control.

It will fly to your back, over your head, aim right at the floor, any direction BUT the way you want it to be. That means when you go into an area with an enemy nearby, chances are you'll mess up.

I'm no stranger to stealth games, action or action-RPG. Never before that I messed up this much. I walked out of cover and got shot. I shot the floor instead of a guard and called in the rest of them. And I even meleed in the wrong direction !?!? All because of this camera issue !!!

I tried it with both joypad and mouse, the problem persisted...
I lowered all the video settings to minimum, the problem still persisted...
I played Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands on the highest video settings without even a hiccup. So I'm sure it's not my machine.

This is not just annoying. It's UNFORGIVABLE.

- Minor flaws for a joypad user. They tie the camera sensitivity to the aiming sensitivity. If you lower the sensivity so you can align your aim better with an analog stick, the camera turning speed will get dragged down to a crawl.
But if your camera turns with a moderate speed, it will be VERY difficult to align your shot to a small target.

In conclusion:
The game has a lot of potentials. But the developer ruined it all with LOUSY camera controls. If you can endure the frustration, this might not be a bad game for you.

The core gameplay doesn't change much and there's nothing wrong with it. They've added some new moves and mini-games. That's a nice touch. Multi-player froze my console once, so I didn't get my hands on it much.

The controls can be clunky and annoying, especially the target locking. You'll mess up quite a lot of your quick or stealth kills because of it. You might feel like you're getting old and clumsy along with Ezio. For me, that strangely adds the feeling to the game, though it gets me upset sometimes.

However, one SERIOUS flaw that bashes this game down to 3 stars is that there's a loop hole which makes you stuck and can't progress pass the Memory Sequence 3 - Guild Contracts mission in a single player mode.

In this Memory Sequence, the game will force you to send one assassin on a mission as a part of a tutorial. If you play only the main story missions up to this point, there's no problem. You'll have a Level-11 assassin to send on a contract mission (the pigeon coup thing, as in AC: Brotherhood) as required.

BUT, as I had spent 12+ hours before this mission to open the map, set up shops, fight for territories, and order my assassins around, that made the level of my assassins go up to Level 12. The Guild Contracts mission didn't acknowledge my assassins since they were one level too high. (Yeah, sorry, your men are too strong. They'll fail the mission.) And once you interact with a Pigeon Coup, the game doesn't let you back out until you finish this tutorial.

That means, if you don't have an EXACT Level-11 assassin, you'll get stuck in an infinite loop, AKA Limbo.

I tried look up a solution on the internet. Sadly, none of them worked for me.
Quitting to-and-fro Animus Island didn't do anything.
I couldn't recruit any new low-level assassin since I had captured all the Templar Dens and did the Den Defense mini-games to a high level already.
I had waited for the Templar to re-capture the Dens, but no luck either.
* EDIT * The assassin recruiting chance never occurred again.

Finally, after hours of trials and errors, I had to give up, throw away my 12-hour work, and start over a new game.

Gamers will recognize structural elements from Bioshock, which, to my mind, is a very good thing. Here, however, the stealth mechanics work flawlessly, and your magical abilities aren't simply various weapons. Rather, the mechanics allow you to teleport short distances, see through walls (a la Batman, Deus Ex, Assassin's Creed, etc) and inhabit animals and other humans. Not only are these mechanics just cool, they allow you to attack objectives in a multiplicity of ways. DISHONORED is thus a game that can sustain at least a few play throughs.

TIPS:
Get Dark Vision Immediately.
Then Upgrade Blink to level 2.
Then upgrade Agility to 1, as your ability to jump higher will enable higher blinks. Agility 2 is useless.
Then get Bend time. Then STOP time. Stop time costs 8 runes, and it's worth it--especially when you want to kill Tall Boys.

My only gripe would be that the game seems to punish you for being what you are--an assassin-- as killing just a moderate amount of people (in video game reality, obviously) leads to the "dark" ending. To that I ask, who hired the Church Lady as a designer on this thing? I did my best to spare non-combatants, yet the game still seems to take a dim view of killing. And I won't give anything away, but the "dark" ending is not satisfying. I was hoping for at least something bittersweet, like the end of The Searchers.

There's also no barometer to give you real-time data on how much "chaos" you're creating. However, you do get your stats at the end of a mission. So if you're going for the no-kill play through, you ca re-do that mission if you accidentally killed someone. (Unlike Deus Ex, which kept you guessing until the end--Lame.)

It would be good to have some "chaos" gradations in this game. Therefore, you could have a play through with

1. a normal ending (you killed a lot of guys because you're a badasss and they got in your way) but spared civilians, knocked out people when you could and weren't a complete psycho),
2. an ending where you were one of the Super Friends (you killed very few people).
3. a REALLY twisted ending where you played through as a complete homicidal maniac--killing everyone and their pets without compunction and without mercy and often without reason except because there's something wrong with you.

However, I simply played how I wanted--with a fairly strict scorched Earth policy--and watched the "happy" ending on YouTube. Maybe I'll do a no-kill play through at some later point.

But this is pretty nit-picky. Playing the game is really fun. I'm just a little irritated by the end (if you didn't get that).

In conclusion, if you dig first person stealth action games with broad (though not strictly open) worlds, buy this game. It's great.

If you like games where you've got to strategically make your way through an environment, hiding bodies and taking people out without raising the alarm, this is for you.

The mechanics work flawlessly, and the gameplay is where this game shines. At some moments, the experience was not dissimilar to the predator rooms in the Batman games, but the similarities end there. There are lethal and nonlethal takedowns, but your options are the standard fare: guns, dart guns (crossbow), and a variety of grenades. From there, you have many many options for how you want to go about dispatching your victims. There's some refinement of the gameplay from Conviction, but nothing groundbreaking. To that I say, "Does it need to be?" In this case, I'd say no. I could certainly cull elements from other stealth games (disguises, a nanosuit, a more open environment, upgradeable takedowns), but all in all, the decision to refine the core Splinter Cell mechanics proved for a very satisfying stealth experience. Speaking to that, it was also fun to be able to go loud every once in a while. There are some missions where it is essential not to be discovered, and some where it's easier just to open fire. One of the characters in the game tells you what kind of encounters to expect, so you can modify your loadout accordingly beforehand.

Side missions. Are very very fun in this game, and help you to get cash for gear. You're either, killing waves of enemies for a number of rounds until you can be extracted. Or you're sneaking into a compound and may not be detected.

Difficulty. This game is not extraordinarily difficult, if you've played a stealth game or two. In fact, compared to the unforgiving detection mechanics of some earlier splinter cell and MGS games, it's not hard at all. On normal, soldiers generally take a moment to register your presence if you get spotted. This is ample time to either hide or take a quick head-shot.

The plot is serviceable. Bad guys are attacking and Sam Fisher and his team must stop them. There are no real surprises or twists or moments that make you sit up and blink, but it's not ridiculous either. A highlight of the game is the performance by Carlo Rota, whom I recognized from 24. He plays the main villain, Sadiq, and infuses a bit of humor into an otherwise sterile story. Even the iconic Sam Fisher is quite dull. Had the story offered something in the way of drama, I would call Blacklist a solid 5 star game. Just a couple of traitors or satisfying plot-twists would have made this game epic.

Sam's new voice didn't bother me, though considering Sam looks to be about 30 in this game, the reference to his teenage daughter made me chuckle. Speaking of 24, Kiefer Sutherland would have been a good choice. The real problem with Sam here is that the story has no emotional content. There are moments in the game where you decide whether or not to spare of execute people, but these decisions don't factor into the story or how the other characters relate to Sam at all.

So, in conclusion, the core gameplay and stealth mechanics make this game very fun to play, even if the story is somewhat lackluster. I would categorically recommend it to anyone who enjoyed games like Deus Ex or Hitman: Absolution.

Microsoft finally discovered Bluetooth exists and thankfully you can use that or the Xbox wireless dongle on PC too. Battery life is pretty solid and the controller feels good with a clean desktop app to setup your preferences and presets.

Compared to the Razr Wolverine, I'm going to say they trade blows, but I'm going to give this one to the Razr. For the v2, you get wireless, where Razr is just wired - albeit with a long cord. The paddles are marginally better to use than the Razr's buttons. They both have replaceable or swappable sticks/Dpads. For the Wolverine you get a sort of hidden gem in the 'clicky' face buttons. I can't do without them now. Any other controller feels like crap after you use them enough. Plus the controller just seems to fit better in my hands. In comparison, the v2 feels maybe just too small or narrow.

The reason I picked up the v2 was really to have the wireless option. There are complaints about stuck buttons on the v2 going around and that's not unique. I've had that on regular XBO controllers AND my PS5 DualSense. The Razr hasn't had a single issue, but I think some of the feature differences are purely personal preference. If can only afford one option it may come down to wireless or no wireless because I think the Wolverine or whatever new model Razr has is the better controller.

I have been playing LEGO video games since the Star Wars series (Gamecube). These games are nostalgic for me, and each one gets better (except for Lego Batman 2, in which I was not that impressed). Here's a quickie review:

Gameplay: An "improved typical", LM is just like other LEGO games, except that the levels seem longer, and the puzzles are more than force-pulling a switch. The levels aren't half-bad, but the bulk of my joy was for the open New York City hub. Who knew driving taxis in Times Square could be so fun? There are many missions in NYC, and plenty of room to just explore. I could go on and on, but I'll cut it short: I'd buy this game even if it was just the NYC hub.

Controls: The controls are okay, but not the best. For flying characters (such as Nova), I wish the buttons were more intuitive, because some actions that I felt were natural simply were not there. Also, it was a little too easy to go from fighting to flying, and messed up several fights for me. But, the driving feels smooth, and weapon use is good. If anything, Iron Patriot is easily the best character overall.

Wii U Gamepad and Other Things: The use of the gamepad was spot-on. I could use it as a separate screen when playing with a friend, or it became my item/character/mission hub when playing LM alone. No problems there. I was thankful for the non-dynamic split screen option this time around. I hated LEGO Batman 2 because that dynamic split screen slowed everything down, and made me dizzy. But, none of that in this game. *The motion of the game in LM is a little blurry, almost like a movie. It has an 'OFF' option, but that is not totally effective. I still think the camera for LEGO Batman was the best one, and wish it had been kept in later games. C'est la vie.

Overall, this is a great game. It's my favorite since LEGO Batman, and I can't wait to see where LEGO goes from here.

This game is my first foray into Xenoblade. I’ve been a Switch owner since March of 2020 and while I got the usual games such as Mario, Zelda, Pokemon, and so on, I really wanted to try something different than the usual Nintendo standard fare. That game is Xenoblade Chronicles DE.

After watching a little video review I decided to shoot my shot and give this game ago. I’m loving it. I’m not much of a JRPG person, but this game is just awesome and I can see why it’s considered one of the best made in its genre. The world is beautiful. The story has been great. The characters are cool.

The gameplay, I really dig. It’s not turn based (which I’m not that into except for Pokémon), but I’d best compare it to Dragon Age. The main protagonist is Shulk, but the game has a party system where you can have a party of up to 3 character with ones in reserve to swap out and you don’t have to play as Shulk either. Very similar to Dragon Age and the combat itself is also similar. It’s like live action strategy, but you don’t have to spam your basic attack because it’s done automatically by who you are playing as. All you the player have to do is issue commands and use your special abilities. I really like this setup. The only thing I wish this game had though was the ability to switch between characters in your party. You can only do this outside of combat. Aside from that, it’s a very good combat system, but definitely not for everyone.

In regards to the game itself and what there is to do, you got a main story and plenty of side content. The side content involves side quests that center around monster hunts, material gathering, and some with their own little story. I know compared to the original version of this game, they greatly improved on these. The game from my understanding is much more user friendly and convenient now, I for one really like that. Plus looking at comparisons of how the game used to look in combat scenarios, the game looks much more cleaned up. So as definitive editions go, this game is more than just a prettied up port (although in handheld mode the game is not the best looking, so I definitely recommend playing on the big screen if playing on a standard Switch). The devs made some nice quality of life changes as well plus I think there is even new additional story content.

All in all, this is simply a great game and while I haven’t beaten it yet, it’s shaping up to be one of the best games I’ve played and would recommend it to anyone who has play XC1 previously and people into JRPGs. If you’re someone more on the fence, definitely watch some gameplay and check out reviews to see if it might be for you. I will add, I do find this game very accessible. Happy hunting!

Last I recall I’m around 40 hours into this game. Story wise I feel I’m nearing the half point, but I’ve also been putting in the time doing side activities. For anyone who has played the prior games, this’ll be very familiar, but at the same time also new. Each game is in of itself it’s own thing, but XC3 does a great job mixing the old and the new.

Let’s talk battle system. XC3’s is similar much yet simpler than XC2’s and is explained much better. While this game can get overboard on the tutorial side, such as showing how equip gear, it helps immensely with learning the battle system. The devs learned from XC2’s mistakes and fixed them in this game. Now between XC1, 2, & 3, this has been my favorite system. I love that you have the entire main party of characters on the field at once. You can switch during fights. Each character functions a bit differently depending on faction and then class. Stemming from class, this is also the main caveat of this battle system.

For the class system you have three: fighter, healer, and defender. I’d say the names explain themselves. While some characters are certain classes by default, the game let’s you equip whatever class on any character so long as it’s unlocked for them. So you really get a lot of options with how to set your party up. Plus you also get an option at some point for a “hero” letting you add a 7th party member. While the only downside is you can’t control that hero, it gives you sort of a wildcard option on how to build your party. Then there’s the ouroborous system or however it’s spelt where you can unleash a monster of sorts into the battle, but don’t want to give too much away on that as it’s key to the story. So yeah that’s the battle system in a nutshell. I love it. It’s a fun system that I feel offers the player a lot of options with the class system.

Now for story, I haven’t beaten it, but I’m digging it. The game is set in a world where there are two warring factions and certain characters from both sides find themselves coming together to go on an adventure to end that cycle. It’s very much an anti-war game and maybe one of the best I’ve played regarding that subject matter.

Stemming from the story, there’s the new party of characters. Noah, Mio, Eunie, Taion, Lanz, & Sena plus two nopon who are guests of the party. The party system is a major aspect of these games and I find XC3’s to be my favorite bunch so far. The characters seem more realistic and down to earth. While I liked XC2’s party, the characters could get a bit over the top. This game doesn’t have that, they even toned down the nopon in this regard as well. Riku and Manana have been my favorite Nopon main characters of the three games. So yeah I love this party.

Lastly I want to talk about the world. This is a big game with a lot to explore and it all feels very seamless too. Plus there’s plenty of diverse locales. Now what I love most about this game’s world and what makes going through this game intriguing is there is a lot of stuff from prior games. While each game is it’s own thing, anyone who has played both the last two games would know they connect in some way and while I don’t know how XC3 fits in, there’s a lot of things I’ve recognized from previous games. While I don’t think you need to play XC1 and 2 to play XC3, I think it may actually be worth it. Plus the prior two games are great in their own right.

XC3 is an epic JRPG and one of the best games of this year. Yes this year. While it may not get the same hype as games like Forbidden West, Elden Ring, and the upcoming God of War, this one holds its own and will likely be the best game released on the Switch this year. So if you have a Switch and are into JRPGs, highly recommend. Amazing game.

Skyward Sword as a Zelda game is fine. It's an overall enjoyable adventure but is not without it's issues. Some of those issues have been alleviated in this remaster. Others are sadly just as annoying.

To start with, Skyward Sword has some pretty noticeable padding. Throughout the course of the game you will fight the same boss (The Imprisoned) three times with the first and 2nd encounter feeling largely identical.

The game also recycles some areas though these aren't quite as bad as the environment often changes how you approach the area or get around on return trips.

The story is pretty solid as an origin story. There are a number of changes that do make the game more accessible than it had been. For example? You can "Mute" Fi and not have to listen to her saying what the probability of something happening is.

They have added a few other small changes. The ability to skip dialogue is another great little QoL improvement. Finally they added the option to swing Link's Sword with an analog stick versus motion controls. If you never played this back on Wii? It's worth checking out? If you have already played Skyward Sword? It's worth waiting for a sale.

Sports Champions is an interesting game. It's not particularly compelling as a game, but it consists of a generally good set of minigames that provide a tech demo of what the PlayStation Move system can do.

The biggest issue any reviewer faces with this game is that while there is somewhat of a consensus of which games are better than which within the collection of sports offered, I have found that many people simply have different interests. I've told people my opinions before: Table Tennis is the best game; Bocce, Disc Golf, and Gladiator are a lot of fun, if not perfect; Archery is decent but not great; Volleyball falls short of the mark. But I've found that some people simply love volleyball, and don't "get" table tennis. I can't pinpoint the reason, quite frankly, because I don't "get" volleyball. I can play it, but it's not a game I particularly enjoy except as an occasional break from the games I like better.

Each game could have its own review, but none are deep enough to warrant it. (I'll come back to that point later.)

Table tennis seems the most accurate, to me. The paddle on screen moves accurately to represent how you manipulate the Move controller. Spin your Move, and the on-screen paddle spins. Lean it forward, the paddle moves toward the net. Pull the Move away from the Eye, and you take a step back from the table in-game. With some level of accuracy, you can spin the ball as you swing your paddle, much like you would in real life. It's not exactly force-accurate, but swinging the paddle hard causes a hard shot, and lightly tapping the ball means you might not make it over the net.

Disc golf is similar. Angling your hand as you throw angles the disc, allowing you to curve shots appropriately. You need to follow through and release at the right point, just as you would with a real frisbee. The courses aren't particularly inspired, but they're sufficient to play a game with a friend, or championship mode by yourself.

Bocce can be a tricky one, but winds up being a lot of fun if you learn to play it. It controls sort of like how you'd expect to play a bowling game. You can throw the ball or roll it, add sidespin or keep it going straight. Follow through and release at the right point, and you will see pretty close results to what you'd expect.

Volleyball is not as entertaining, to me. You do not control your player's positioning--your player moves on his own. You serve, bump, set, spike, and block using gestures and real movements. I do not play much volleyball, but I have before; I simply found it difficult to perfect the timing used in the game. I also don't enjoy games where I cannot control my character's position, so that's another point against volleyball. Still, many have said they love this game, and I can't say it's without any merit. Two move controllers can be used for this game, but I do not see a huge benefit from doing this, as most of the controls seem more like gestures than 1:1 representations of your hands.

Gladiator duel is a bit more fun, to me. However, it is more fun when played with 2 Move controllers, which not everyone will have. Blocking is done with one Move controller, and attacking is done with the other. You swing your weapon at the enemy and can thrust, slice, or bludgeon as you see fit. Your weapons will closely match your real movements, within reason. With only one controller, a button is used to block, which means you have less complete control over your limbs indepentently. You may just wind up breaking a sweat playing this one, if you get too into it.

Finally, Archery. You can also optionally use two Move controllers for archery. I actually do enjoy it with 2 controllers more, but I'm not sure why. It feels essentially the same, but with an extra arm involved. It's entertaining to do some target shooting and play some of the varied modes. (tic tac toe, moving targets, "tug of war", etc.) Archery has more variety than the other minigames. However, it is not among my favorites, because my arm does get tired from holding it up to fire arrows so much. You have to draw an arrow from your "quiver" (over your shoulder) and hold it up to fire. Fun and innovative, but I'm sure there will be many people with some tired arms. Maybe take a break for some Bocce or Disc Golf between rounds?

Each of these games has a difficulty setting, which generally modifies the enemy AI as well as the assistance the game will provide you. (For instance, a table tennis shot on "gold" may overshoot the table, but on bronze it may land on it due to auto-assist) It's helpful to ramp up the difficulty while you learn the proper motions to play the game. I recommend two Move controllers, if you have them available. If not, you will still get a lot of enjoyment from most of the games. Gladiator is the only one I would say is a lesser game without a second Move controller.

The one thing that disrupts gameplay, in my opinion, is the unnecessarily long load times. The environments are relatively simple, all things considered, and starting a match should not take as long as it does. Having to recalibrate the Move often doesn't help, but it's not as terrible as the load times. I was hoping this would be patched, but it never was. So, be prepared to take a breather--you might appreciate it if playing an exerting game, but for the most part the load times are unwelcome.

At the current price, even though this is an older Move title, this should be in every Move owner's collection of games. It's not a full game with story and depth, but it is an entertaining if shallow experience. Playing with friends makes it even more entertaining. If you're not familiar with a sport, that's okay--there are tutorials to provide information on the rules of each game, including tips for how far to stand from the TV, and other advice. Sports Champions offers a good tech demo of what the Move is capable of. Hopefully we'll see more titles that use the controller as well as this game does, but I haven't seen many yet.

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. Where do I begin? And where do I end? The beauty of it is that while I may begin and end at the same place, the journey there can vary endlessly.

Having never played any other Elder Scrolls games, I cannot judge how much of an upgrade or advancement this is from Oblivion and Morrowind. I cannot tell you how the combat system is different, or how much prettier this game is relative to the previous ones.

What I can tell you is that this is a fantastic game, admittedly with some issues, that is worth a look from anyone interested in a huge, immersive world, an arching storyline, endless sidequests, and quite simply a good time.

I can't say much that hasn't already been said, unfortunately. The game is beautiful. The graphics are very good--they may not be the best I've seen, but taking a step back and looking at a gorgeous landscape on high quality, I find it hard to believe you wouldn't at least be somewhat impressed. (Unless you wouldn't marvel at the Grand Canyon or Niagara Falls, in real life. In which case, I doubt much impresses you visually)

The world is massive, and alive. There are plenty of people to interact with. Some will ask you to do a series of deep quests that have nothing to do with the main storyline. Others will be of no use to you at all. Quite simply, it's like a real world. People run out of money. People try to leverage you for their will. (sometimes against each other) You will make choices. Some will matter, some won't be too relevant.

You could finish the storyline quickly, and enjoy the game. To get the most out of it, it's a good idea to explore the world. See more of it, and interact with more NPCs.

Leveling up in this game isn't the same as in a standard RPG. You have a character level, but your skills also have their own individual levels. Leveling your skills up contributes to leveling your character up, which gives you points to assign to skill bonuses, as well as an increase health, magic, or stamina. This makes leveling much less of a grind, because your character level itself doesn't offer as much benefit as in most games. You increase your skill levels simply by using them--forging bracers increases your smithing skill, and blocking attacks with your shield increases your blocking skill, for instance.

The combat is less than stellar. It's something I still don't particularly enjoy--it feels a bit rigid and restrained, sometimes even awkward. Swings of your sword just don't feel as satisfying as I'd like, and switching weapons during combat is hindered by some awkward controls, as well. Character controls overall are acceptable, but could use some improvement. If you get past the combat (which is admittedly a large part of gameplay, for most people), then the rest of the game can truly shine.

The most apparent shortcoming of this game, as many will tell you, is its menu system. It was created for a controller rather than a keyboard/mouse, which is quite apparent the entire time. Questionable decisions were made in many ways--the amount of space to dedicate to the image vs the item text/description, the number of items that can be seen at the same time, lack of proper sorting, and various other problems plague menus throughout the game. Navigating through the perk assignment screen when you level up is atrocious, as well. There are times when pressing up/down/left/right (w/a/s/d) will simply not go to the next logical item on this menu. This may not make sense, but the perk assignment menus are shaped like constellation, so the next perk may be diagonally up/right, but sometime neither up nor right will actually select the next perk--instead they will skip it or move to the next tree of skills. It is confusing and makes absolutely no sense. Visually appealing? Maybe. But it's about as intuitive as the game ET was for the Atari 2600. (Read: not even the least bit)

Overall, while the menus are a big part of the game, they do not break the experience. The PC version of Skyrim has an advantage, of being moddable. Mods have already been created to modify the UI a bit. I have not tried any of these mods yet--my experience has only been with the original product as released by Bethesda. Still, I have to say this is one of the more appealing games of 2011. The world can just suck you in. On a day where I didn't have any specific plans, I spent hours without even realizing it, barely looking up except to get a drink or use the bathroom. It is an excellent game, and while there are some significant flaws, it should not be completely overlooked based on these flaws--the overall product shines through, once you learn your way around the menus, combat, and the game world.

I strongly encourage anyone who has a PC, 360, or PS3 to check this one out. The PC has the advantage of being moddable, but the title is likely to impress regardless of which system you play it on, as long as you give it enough time to pick up its pace.

Well, Cyberpunk 2077 finally got me to want to once again future proof/upgrade my PC specs. Me trying to play this at the minimum specs suggested by CDPR was the wake-up call I needed. It's time to finally throw in the towel for my i5-4690K and DDR3 RAM. Now, I fully understand how perplexing it is to think one current game (regardless if it's buggy or not) should not be the deciding factor for this situation, but it's clear I shouldn't be constantly messing with settings at every noticeable visual (and audio) distraction when my CPU bottlenecks. I upgraded my GPU when CoD:MW (2019) landed, and now it's finally time for the rest now that Cyberpunk 2077 is here...and for future games. Like seeing a glimpse of Raytracing, or what I call the "the could be's." Yeah, I want to make my PC copy of this game look smooth and beautiful as hell.

But when it comes to the gameplay specifically, I personally believe there is something great within Cyberpunk 2077...but OH MOMMA it needs more fine tuning. Every enemy encounter or even dialogue scenario, something feels amiss. As of right now, I don't think this game (possibly post patch-DLC fashion) will ever be as great as that first impression I had about launch of Witcher 3. Pre-established narrative pieces probably helped with my biasing then, but I remember being thoroughly impressed by that current state of the RED engine then (even Witcher 2). Not particularly graphical issues, but in comparison to narrative, side quests, world design, CDPR seem to want to show off spectacle or ambitious set pieces instead of actual fully playable RPG scenarios. About 10 hours was when I finally got to that current-ish Deus Ex feel I was expecting from this game. It was then when I finally noticed that the character progress had positive and negatives in the grand PVE design. And honestly, I still think that Deus Ex did it better in multiple playthroughs I put into that series. So when bugs and glitches come into discussion on this game, this is when I really start to ask about the development. It's like CDPR forgot to fine tune these elements to the fullest because they were more concerned about ensuring a NPC's mechanical augments looking great with RTX on, or how how the street lights shimmer off of your car when moving.

Speaking of driving, so far vehicle handling feels worse (like GTA IV worse). Also, I can't be the only one who thinks some of the sexual content (either for humor or seriousness) feels a little to "try hard" like? In GTA, everything was a satire since that was the point. Here, I kind of roll my eyes because the game constantly keeps hitting you over the head with it in areas where you kind of shouldn't expect to see over sexualization, or something? either it's the same advertisement you keep seeing or the jokes (when it is one) really aren't that funny to begin with. But if I have to pin-point down my biggest complaint turned future playthroughs concern, it's the Shorter campaign idea. I was all for this idea at first due to there are 3 life paths for your prologue. Color me spoiled by something like Dragon Age: Origins, because so far I have yet to see why even choosing a life path effects really anything substantial to the game plot outside of just a few dialogue scenarios. To be blunt, it feels a bit too Mass Effect like. It was probably intended this way, but I out of the 2 life paths I've played through, I still think you converge on the main plot path (meet Jackie) way too soon for my tastes. Unless later on (or I just missed it), I have yet to see why choosing Street punk over Nomad or Corporate really matters for my character. Gun combat feels as it should for this type of game, thought there is A LOT of visual flair that keeps popping up in the HUD (yes I get it was intended) but it feels too distracting to some moments. Thankfully there is a colorblind mode as A LOT of that RED flaring up was a bit much for myself. If you choose to go melee, you really see the blemish. CDPR needs to patch up in this department ASAP, because it plays out pretty finnicky. Maybe my aptitude towards this will change the longer I play, and figure out the moe optimal RPG progression...well, you know if I can stop messing my graphical settings that is.

So at the end of the day, would I suggest this game? It depends. If you have the PC specs to enable Raytracing for least at 60FPS (or can only scrounge up for at least a Xbox Series X), yes. Go for seeing one of the most beautiful and dynamic current/next gen open-world RPG games available now. It does take a bit for the Deus Ex like to fully kick in and I'm sure you could let this crazy world envelop you for sure. HOWEVER it's clear as day that the game should have been delayed even further. You will see the caveats many have mentioned at some point. Which brings us to the big topic about CDPR currently: Within the 5-8 years of development, why is it in this state for current PC and even previous Gen owners (the ones they originally advertised for)? It's clear as day that they should have come out and admitted that base PS4 and Xbox One S-X consoles can't handle this game. They should have just bit the bullet, and made a push with at least XBox Series S/X and PS5 there. It probably would have tarnished their reputation even more, but more focus could have gone into ensure those platforms (including various PC configurations) were optimally working at least, or fine tuning to the RPG elements within the game.
At this rate I rather have Cyberpunk 2077 struggle on my current PC only because of my current specs, if that meant everything else was actually working and everything else advertised by CDPR was actually included in the product. And that goes for base PS4s and XboxOnes. This game is so undercooked it hurts. Cyberpunk 2077 is definitive proof that letting money talk before you're actually finished can tarnish a IP...and a beloved developer. We just had to have on more annoyance from 2020.

Monster Hunter Rise is literally hitting everything that I liked about the previous release (World) in a specifically made for handheld-play experience for the Nintendo Switch. Yes, graphics do looks like a downgrade in comparison, but the fluidity of combat and animation detail is still present in a much more straight to the point MH-experience for newcomers and veterans of the series. Instead of being a direct port for the game, Capcom built this game for the Switch, and optimized it accordingly utilizing the always wonderful RE Engine.

The new additions like switch-skills for weapons and wirebugs movement abilities have literally made the gameplay/combat some of the best boss-fight experiences I've ever played in a video game. One of last things I did in this was achieve a first attempt/one-shot hunt on a particular annoying monster, Rajang using the iconic Great Sword. The experience and the high I got from that achievement was like conquering a video-game version of PTSD...since I had a hell of a time with his version from World (my first MH game ever). I've put in 61 hours then and still so far and I can't get enough of it.

Rise is worth getting now, or if you wait for the PC release; meaning the gameplay experience could only get better on PC with expected graphical enhancements. But for a handheld game now, I agree with Eurogamer that it's literally the best Switch release since Breath of the Wild in terms of relatability and performance. While I do constantly go back to Smash Bros with the family and still enjoy the crap out of Mario Odyssey in both switch modes, I legit can't get enough of MHRise. It'll be worth whatever price you pay for it on whatever platform you choose.

Since the Nintendo 64‘s release, the video game company Nintendo has released a Fighting Game Series called Super Smash Bros. Games where Nintendo characters such as Mario, Luigi, Samus Aran, Ness, Link, Zelda, Pikachu, and many others would enjoy brawl matches between themselves. And since the amazing Super Smash Bros Brawl game on the Wii, more characters from other consoles and Nintendo games have joined the fighters ranks. Solid Snake, Pokemon Trainer, Lucario, Greninja; though among my two favourites are Shulk of Xenoblade Chronicles and Bayonetta from the series Bayonetta.

In this game made for the Nintendo Switch, Super Smash bros Ultimate offer many game content for fans and newcomers. Online brawls, Smash matches with eight players, Mob Smash, Tourneys, Special Smash with twisted obstacles, online matches with worldwide participants, challenges, and story modes. And for that latter aspect, players get a great jackpot. A storyline called World of Light, with all heroes fighting off two armies of darkness and light led by formidable opponents. A game where we explore two worlds. One of Light, another of Darkness. Where we reassemble characters together and advance through fights that allow us to collect spirits linked to popular Nintendo series, but also obscure/neglected ones like Eternal Darkness and Hotel Dusk. Two universes I love, alongside those of Mother whose first and third games really deserve a proper release on Nintendo 3DS or on the Switch. Just like these other classics that need more attention from the public.

So for this World of Light storyline, we get a wide exploration and battle on major platforms linked to many games universes we love. But on the downside, I wish that the game director and producers could have offered us cinematics between the characters. Sequences that would happen either before/after the fights, or in between spirits and the playable characters they are friends with. That would have brought us back to the beauty of Super Smash Bros Brawl‘s story mode on Wii. As we saw in that Wii game emotional connections between the characters that were absent in the Switch. Connections revealing the complicity and rivalry amongst the crew. So if there ever were a new game in the Smash Bros series, I hope we will get cinematic moments between characters in the game story mode. More than funny or epic photos we can obtain if we accomplish certain achievements.

As for the Classic Mode, an individual storyline for each character; fights set according to certain persons related to his/her life. Either another playable character, or a Major Spirit Opponent (ex: Dracula if we fight as Simon or Richter Belmont). A storyline that concludes with a nice hunt for points through the end credits. Culminating with a funny picture. Though again, I’d wish interactive cinematics would have been offered for these adventures.

Apart from these narrative gameplays, fans of game designs will enjoy creating their own stages in the Stage Builder and sharing them online, just like they will love training their own Amiibo figures they have purchased in stores. Another great initiative for fans of Mii players are their chance to design their Mii’s suit. Wearing costumes from all series (Super Mario, Fire Emblem, Legend of Zelda, etc.)

Now for the gameplay of Super Smash Bros, the camera angles are the same as in all Smash games. Wide angles that cover the entire stage, which may be cumbersome or confusing for certain gamers. So those who’d prefer their brawl matches with much closer angles may find it cumbersome to play a Smash bros game series and might want to pass.

As for the music, Masahiro Sakurai, Yoshino Aoki and Hideki Sakamoto composed a nice range of melodies for the game. Making it grandious, epic. And the addition of tunes from the games mentionned in that console are another great chance for fans to discover of relisten to their tracks.

In sum, Super Smash Bros Ultimate is a wonderful chapter in that Nintendo game series and a must if you own a Nintendo Switch.

And with the upcoming new characters like Banjo Kazooie and those from Dragon Quest, fans of those two series will be sure to enjoy this fighting-brawl game.

Following South Park The Stick of Truth‘s success, where Trey Parker and Matt Stone, creators of the show South Park, had complete creative control, the game needed a sequel. One with equal quality as in the first one, while pushing through new creativity & content. And for that they released two great games. First, South Park‘s Phone Destroyer, which I shall review eventually, then The Fractured But Whole, which covers an important current in American Cinema today.

Super Heroes movie franchises.

Movies praised for their high special effects and for connecting families multi-age audiences, but criticised for their bombastic formulas, their unsubtle/moralising/preachy SJW messages, and commercialistic opportunism. Which has been denounced in certain Marvel Comics films like Captain Marvel. Although this criticism has been mostly absent from the DC franchise as movies like Wonder Woman have tried to focus on their stories and not on a political agenda. Although if one criticism still remains strong, it is the commercial business behind these super hero films.

Which is what the storyline in Fractured But Whole tries to satirise. In a game where the New Kid, after his adventures in Stick Of Truth and Phone Destroyers, participates in the Super Hero adventures within the South Park Community. Developping an identity as The Farting Vigilante. Discovering the rival camps between the “Coon and Friends” and “Freddom Pals” teams as they attempt to launch their specific movie franchises. And fighting crime around South Park as many South Park cats have disappeared. And behind this drama hides an evil antagonist who exploits others as puppets; in his games of money and power.

So through this game, Trey Parker and Matt Stone entertain us with a hilarious story that further explores South Park’s mentality and satirises Super Hero culture. Always subtly, never trying to overpreach a message. While introducing new characters from the latest seasons. Such as PC Principal and his SJW tactics that players can use to defend themselves during fights. Like they can also summon special individuals who can attack enemies; though they do not completely vanquish them like in Stick of Truth, nor are they usable only once per day. Instead, they can be summoned at a specific number of times during the entire game, or if certain items are crafted.

Indeed, another function offered in Fractured But Whole is “Crafting”. Where you conceive items strengthening your powers, defend you in fights, heal you, or even design costumes for your Super Hero Identity. Ability which grows the more you craft items and collect junk during fights, and while you walk around levels or purchase items in stores.

In sum, a creative customisation that integrates itself into the story. And it is nice how the game’s cinematics retranspose on your character your costume design. As it makes the game more personalised, following your creative and design interests.

For the gameplay, players still move around a South Park environment that corresponds to the one on TV, as if we were interacting in an actual episode of the show. Though for the fights, the game levels are different. Not using a RPG turn based attacks mode, but a board game platform like in Super Robot Taisen and Fire Emblem, with players moving and attacking like Chess figures. So every move can either help you or hamper your battle. Furthermore, your attacks may be infinite and not rely on Power Points, but the way you interact in the fight can have an impact on your victory or defeat.

So in its game content, South Park Fractured But Whole offers a new interaction mode with the characters and their environments. While presenting an interesting storyline that details more about the New Kid and his family, whose turmoils reach a critical tension as both parents argue constantly regarding their son and his Super abilities; while refusing any dialogue with him about their past. Which makes me wonder what does the father do for a living? Let’s hope another South Park game answers that question one day. Just like they introduce further DLC contents as interesting as the ones we have. Indeed, the game presents as first DLC level a Vampire story set in the actual Casa Bonita restaurant, popular in Denver and worldwide thanks to South Park who did an episode about it. Through this level, an adorable way to discover the culture of this restaurant whose attractions look fascinating and worthy to visit one day. A level that also offers an awesome tribute to a legendary pop culture figure, which delighted that artist’s fans a lot.

Then, as second DLC Level, a Friday the 13 like tribute on the horror movie genre, set at Lake Tardicaca and featuring Mint Berry Crunch, a super hero whom I wish could have had a presence as well in the game’s Cthulhian side-story as Mint Berry Crunch first appeared in a South Park episode satirising HP Lovecraft’s classics.

Still, the completion of these DLC levels allow you to add Mint Berry Crunch into your super hero team for your main storyline, alongside another character I will not name, but whom fans like a lot as she becomes playable during the Casa Bonita adventure and into your main story.

Finally, there is the customizable Virtual Reality fights of Professor Timothy, allowing you to revisit past antagonists or new ones in particular battle situations, Obtaining bonuses and certain items as victory results.

For the soundtrack of Fractured But Whole, Jamie Dunlap and Scott Nickoley did fantastic compositions. Melodies and tunes that follow the musicography of the South Park show. Employing original tunes from the show, but also new tracks. Grandiose melodies that show how the artists behind South Park have always been attentive to their projects’ music. Which makes sense as they were behind the successful Book of Mormon musical.

For the voice actors, the same original cast records voices. And if you enjoy the show in different languages, you can also obtain a French and Spanish dub. Though regarding the French voice work, I wish it had the original French dubbers like Christophe Lemoine as Cartman for their performances were unique, to a point some francophone fans preferred listening to the show in French rather than English. Whereas for this game, the voices we have here are unmemorable.

Nevertheless, South Park Fractured But Whole is a must if you are a fan of the show, but also enjoy playing unconventional video games that make you question your surroundings, while never trying to preach an unsubtle message. Which too many USA entertainment films/shows attempt today, but do so quite badly and people don’t embark into their agenda.
