Ever since we bought our first Wii years ago we have been waiting for them to transfer this game into the Wii platform. When I saw that it was coming out this fall I was SO excited and hoped that I wouldn't be disappointed. Well... I'm not! This game is wonderfully versatile. It is difficult enough that my husband and I cannot beat all of the levels on the first try, and that's just beating it, not trying to collect every little puzzle piece and extra bonus.

Yet, the makers of the game were smart enough to not scare away their littlest customers by adding a neat little thing called "Super Guide". When you get to mid-point it pops up this little pig looking thing that has a thought bubble that is the plus sign button on the remote. If you push that button while you are standing near the pig he puts it in super guide mode. A silver gorilla goes through and completes the entire level while you watch and see exactly how to finish it. The bonus is that once he has finished going, the level is actually complete. When finished with a level it gets a colored dot over it, red if Super Guide did it and blue if you are the one that did it. Genius! Then you can go back and do the levels that stump you without feeling stressed and stuck!

They also allow you to have several games saved at one time so each person can have their own at their own pace. It is 2 player, but like Super Mario Bros for Wii if one of the players goes too far ahead on the screen it drags the other person along and can kill them if they are in a bad area. 2 player is definitely not recommended in playing with young children because they don't pay attention to where you are at.

I think the makers of this game added just enough Wii controllability to make it new and fun but left enough of the original intact that we don't feel like it's a completely new thing. The hardest thing for me to master was the roll, having to hold the nunchuk button sideways while pounding my hands didn't feel like a natural movement to make him roll.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone that loved DKC back in the 90s or just anyone that loves a new challenge on the Wii!

One of the most iconic characters in video game history has to be Mario. From the traditional side scrolling games to other ventures such as puzzle and RPG games there is nothing this plumber hasn’t been in. Now a new title is going to be released on the Wii U called Super Mario 3D world. But is this going to be a great successor to the franchise or should you just pop in the original Super Mario Bros?

The game starts as Luigi, Mario, Toad and Princess Peach are exploring the Mushroom Kingdom when they come across a pipe. The pipe isn’t the traditional green one it is clear and while inspecting it a green fairy creature pops out. It introduces itself as a Sprixie but before learning more about this creature Bowser shows up and kidnaps it and jumps into the pipe. Mario and friends jump in after Bowser as they are now in the Sprixie kingdom as they are search for her and her companions.

Playing the game is similar to the other 3D games as you can wander around freely but each of the characters have different abilities. You can jump higher and fall slower as Luigi, Mario has average speed and jump height, Peach can float in mid air but not run as fast, Toad runs really fast but cannot jump as high.

Powerups are a real important part of any of the Super Mario games and this one has loads that you can use to your advantage. But there are new powerups such as a cat costume (that has it’s own attacks and allows you to climb walls), double cherries (that allow you to create a clone of yourself) and Goomba masks that allows you to blend in and not be attacked by enemy Goombas.

Also one player can use the Gamepad to not only touch the screen to hinder enemies and aid players but to reveal hidden blocks and items. This game also supports Off-TV Play so you can take this game with you on the small screen.

This is a wonderful entry into the Super Mario universe and if you have a Wii U you need to purchase this game. With tons of new powerups, great controls and new worlds to explore this is the game that fans have been waiting for.

When I got my Playstation 3 there were two games that I purchased with it. The first was Gran Turismo 5 prologue and the other was Killzone 2. I thought that this would be just another first person shooter but it turned out to be a great game. Now with the release of the Playstation 4 one of the same day releases is a game called Killzone Shadowfall. But is this a game that you will want to get at launch or should you wait for a better game?

This game takes place thirty years after the events of Killzone 3. It focuses on the conflict between the Helghast and the Vektans and these are two rivals who are trying to colonize a distant planet. For thirty years these two factions have been living side by side separated by a giant wall. There has been a fragile peace that has existed for this time but it seems to be eroding as both factions are on edge.

You play as Lucas Kellan who is a member of the Shadow Marshals (a military intelligence unit) who tries to keep the peace between these two factions. The missions will vary from stealthy infiltrations to all out firefights. You will have various weaponry at your disposal ranging from your standard pistols and rifles to sniper rifles and even a drone. The drone is called an OWL as it can not only attack enemies but also hack terminals and shield you from incoming attacks.

There is also going to be more content released for this game as there is a $20 season pass available. This gives access to co-op play , new map packs and two additional multiplayer expansion packs. The multiplayer aspect of the game has been tweaked for the better as there are three classes for players to choose from. Assault, Support and Scout are the three classes and each of these have special abilities that you can deploy. For example the assault class has a buddy drone that will automatically attack incoming enemies. There are 10 maps that are going to be available at launch and more will be released in the coming months.

If you are a fan of the Killzone games and were lucky to get a PS4 then this is the essential game to get.

My 5 year old son liked the first Knack game so we decided to try this one as well. This is MUCH better in so many ways:

-- longer time to beat the entire game (though not by much) ... probably 30-40 hours total for the whole game
-- the game play itself is better, with the option to shrink down to mini-Knack and then re-grow to original size at any time (this helps you get around obstacles, climb up smaller areas, etc). This makes the game more fun but also more complicated. That said, my 5 year old can handle it so you probably can too.
-- multi-player mode (NOT online) has been improved a thousand fold: both characters are just as important and can both do basically the same things (except when "driving" cars or robots, in which case P1 controls where you're going as well as one attack button, while P2 generally has to aim and shoot missiles as well as one or two other attacks). The camera tries to keep both players in view, though at times, one player will have more control than the other (it's not always P1 who takes priority)
-- the puzzles are mostly easy but some take a little while to figure out. The game offers hints in such situations which is nice. We've never needed to use the hints so i'm not sure how handy they actually are.
-- secrets - there are still secret rooms with treasures to open up (same as in the first game), but there are much fewer this time around. Additionally, when you pause the game, it shows how many secrets are available vs how many you've already found (most areas have 2-3 secrets).
-- levels are pretty straight forward and you do not really have an option to go one way or the other (you can do it rarely, but it ends up being a dead end with a secret).

The only big negative is that there are a bunch of glitches throughout the game: the entire game completely crashed once, we got "stuck" at a spot with no way out another time, and all of the cut scenes towards the last few hours of game play were skipped (it just showed a black screen for 5 seconds and then continued with the game).

This is a cute game and good for kids and adults, though if you're an adult, don't expect a huge challenge (we're playing on normal mode, maybe hard mode would be better for grown ups - idk) and even with the glitches, i would recommend it .... if you're playing in 2 player mode, the first Knack isn't even worth it - just play this one instead.

I've only played for 2 days, but I'm enjoying this quite a bit.

The game play is pretty easy:
You jog through various lands. You squeeze on the ring fit to "air blast" things near you (ie: open a door, break a box). You pull on the ring fit to "vacuum" things (ie: bring coins to you), and also to jump (you blast downwards for this). Most of the time, you don't actually NEED to do this, but I find it fun to try to collect all of the items so I could level up sooner.

I find the direction controls annoying. For example, if something is located at the 10 O'Clock position from me, it's hard to judge where to point the ring fit in order to actually blast that exact direction. I'm only on day 2 though, so it's quite possible that I'll get better at this as time goes on.

The game also has monsters that you have to beat. This is done with "exercise contest" in an RPG style. You can either choose the attack that you wish to use, or use a random one. You will then need to do a set of that chosen exercise, and the monster's health bar will decrease. You then choose the next attack. Most monsters need at least 2-3 different exercises.

As your level rises, you gain more hearts, more attack damage & defend power, and more exercises to use in the battles.

My 8 year old son is also enjoying this game quite a bit. The game chose our starting strength level automatically based on our ages, some easy questions (do you exercise right now or not?), and how strong our initial "squeeze" of the ring fit was. As far as I could tell, the strength level is the amount of reps you have to do for each exercises in the monster battles.

I hate exercising, but this feels more like a game and I don't really think of it as hard work (even though I do feel sore after using it)

I recommend this to anyone who wants to work out, without feeling like they're working out.

In the year 2011, Skyrim was the positively received by users of the Playstation 3; Batman: Arkham City was the most popular game for the Xbox 360. But for the Nintendo Wii, the most popular game released was The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword.

For owners of the Nintendo Wii, last year was a bit of a bumpy ride. Rather than focus on their home console, Nintendo paid more attention to their new handheld console: the Nintendo 3DS. With the Wii's recent downfall in the amount of new games being created for it and the announcement of the Nintendo Wii U, things were looking down for the Nintendo Wii. However, with the arrival of The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword, Nintendo makes their final attempt at keeping the Wii alive.

This large, ever-expanding Wii game packs in so much into one little disc. Because I'm personally not one to jump directly into a game, I found it slightly annoying how large the game really was--as I'm not one to play video games for hours on end.

While Skyward Sword can take hours to fully complete, all the many multiple features this game includes calls for a great replay value. I say this because you'll most likely find yourself replaying it over and over again to find hidden treasures you hadn't seen before. To this day I'm still finding objects around the world this game offers me.
The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is the first 3D Zelda game I've ever owned. This being said, I'm not going to make any connections between this game and Ocarina of Time, The Wind Waker, etc.

In terms of the storyline, the Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword takes place before any of the games in the Legend of Zelda franchise. The story begins when we're introduced to a land in the sky known as Skyloft. Link--the protagonist of our epic journey and the character you will be playing as--is on his way to celebrate the "Wing Ceremony", a tradition in which he hopes to acquire the label of a Skyloft knight.

In order to become a knight, Link enters a race on a bird-like creature called a Loftwing. After you win the race, Zelda--who hasn't even reached the title of "princess" at this point--awards you with a sailcloth; later in the game, this sailcloth will be used as a parachute multiple times throughout the game.

Not too long after Link gains his knighthood he and Zelda are caught in a storm while riding on her Loftwing. Before she can escape, Zelda falls of her Loftwing and makes her way into the land below Skyloft: the unexplored surface.

When Link tells Zelda's father about his daughter's disappearance, he is given knight's clothes. Any fan of the Zelda franchise will recognize this uniform as the green, medieval clothes Link wears in every other Legend of Zelda game. From then on Link makes his way down to the surface and goes on a journey to save his friend.

The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword can only be played with the Wii motion plus controller+Nunchuk combo. This being said, you won't be able to play the game with your standard Wii remote. Thankfully for me, my copy of Skyward Sword came with the golden Wiimote with motionplus controls.

By pressing down the A button on your remote, you can make Link move faster with any action he performs. In order to be certain that players won't abuse this, Nintendo added a circular gauge that shows up whenever you use the A button. When this gauge empties, Link will huff and puff and will be rendered too weak to work until the gauge refills itself within a matter of about five seconds.

Holding down the B trigger at the back of your remote will allow you to select a tool to use--whether that tool be your slingshot, your bow, your bug net, etc.

Holding down the C button on your nunchuk will allow you to enter your "Dowsing" position, where you'll enter a first-person mode that helps you when looking for people by giving you a radar attribute. By using the motion controls can you point yourself in the direction of who you're looking for while in your "Dowsing" mode.

As has been the case with every 3D Zelda game--ever since Ocarina of Time--you have the option of locking onto your enemies. In this game, however, you do so by pressing the Z button on your nunchuk. Whenever a person, monster, or a specific object with is within your reach, you can press the Z button to lock onto and interact with them. If there is not anything you can interact with nearby, pressing the Z button will only shift the camera directly behind Link.

Now for my favorite control of the whole game: the sword controls. Much like the case with many other sword games for the Wii--such as the Red Steel series--you control your sword by swinging your remote around. Thanks to the motion plus you are given when you receive this game, you can thrust your sword in nine directions.

These nine methods of thrusting of your sword can have an impact on how effective your attacks are. For example: a lot of enemies will be able to parry your attacks by holding up a defender at a specific angle. In order to combat against these defensive strategies, you will have to swing your Wiimote in the opposite direction to which your enemy's defender is at. This method of attack calls for much more interaction and strategy to come into your gameplay.

For people who want to kill off their foes with fewer hits, you have the option of unleashing the true power of your sword. Simply by pointing your Wiimote up, Link will follow your action and point his sword "Skyward".

Once skyward, your sword will start to charge up with energy. After a matter of about three seconds, your sword will be completely charged up. However, it won't remain charged up for long--so you'll have to use your energy before too long. But when you do use it, a ring will skyrocket from your sword and cut through almost everything in its way. This is a great way to fend off and defeat enemies in a matter of seconds.

I found The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword to be a very enjoyable Wii game. I recommend any Wii owner to pick up a copy of Skyward Sword. Its vast, ever-expanding world will keep you on your toes for hours--not to mention all the action and strategy. While I personally found the game a bit too large for my taste, I'm sure many others will agree that this is still a fantastic game.

If you own a Nintendo Wii and you have plenty of time on your hands, I recommend you at least try this out and see if you like it yourself.

Okay; I'll be honest. The Nintendo Gamecube controller is one of the most comfortable controllers I have ever held in my own two hands. Its ergonomic design, unique button layout, and shoulder buttons make me feel like I'm holding onto a sturdy, reliable piece of hardware. But why did I give this only FOUR out of FIVE stars, screaming Nintendo fanboys? Well, let's see....

For one thing, the Gamecube controller itself is very easy to break in terms of sturdiness. Unlike other controllers--like the Nintendo Wii remote and the Xbox 360 controller--bending this controller by its handles can cause a loud screech of rubbing plastic to vibrate in your ears. This fears me as to how long this controller will really last.

In addition to a lack of sturdiness, some features given to other controllers of its era are missing with the Nintendo Gamecube controller. For one thing, the joysticks don't click when you press down--a feature that was added to the Dualshock 2 controller for the Playstation 2. Finally there's the embarassingly tiny d-pad, which is so tiny I can actually fit its entirety under either of my already-small thumbs.

But honestly, those last two reasons are just nitpicks to say the least. Everything else about this controller is just fine. If you own a Wii or Gamecube, try picking up one of these controllers.

This game ranks up there with MLB the Show as one of the best sports games I have ever played. Baseball probably translates easier to digitized form, but Konami has gone above and beyond with this years edition of their beautiful game.

To put it simply, there are only a few flaws in this game and I'll list them here.
- Firstly the presentation is bad, period. The PS3 menus exhibit lag, at least when using the disc version, uninstalled. The commentary is horrendous, and the new MyClub mechanics are pretty confusing and the tutorial isn't of much help. Fortunately, these things are not gameplay related.
- Secondly, PES has always relied on community Edit Files to bring in corrected kits and teams/players, and this remains the same this year as the Premier League is unlicensed with the exception of Man United (who are missing their 3rd blue kit in the game btw) and the Bundesliga is a noticeable omission as well, although Bayern and and I believe Leverkusen are in.

Now comes the positives, and the inevitable comparisons to Fifa:
- This year's game finally removes the robotic dribbling from the older versions. In fact, although the overall animations are not as good as Fifa, certain player animations are actually better (Messi, Ronaldo, and especially Robben) due to Konami's Player ID animation. Robben's arms are lifted high just like in real life.
- The editing and tactics are much more in detailed than Fifa's. Fifa has always been a "take it or leave it proposition," being EA's vision, whereas PES makes the game your vision. The tactics go above and beyond anything you'll find in Fifa.
For example, you have Offensive, Defensive, and Custom tactics, each of these allowing for 3 formations respectively (for kickoff, with possession, and without possession). That means you can set up 6 (because I don't count the kickoff formation) in game formations that can fluidly transition one to the other by using PES' "Fluid Formations" setting.
- Finally, this game plays like the real game of football, with lots of passing and build-up play. Manual shooting is great, assigning manual runs is great, and the unexpected goals and tackles are great. Speed is still important but not more so than accurate passing and skilled dribbling is also important but skilled dribbling here is about close control rather than tricks.

I entered all three DLC locations and as of May 2016 I was invaded in Sunken King, and I was summoned in Iron King, so there is at least still some multiplayer activity. The difficulty is quite high but the experience is fun and tense just like the base game.

Final point: this is a better deal than digital keys if the cost of this disc is actually lower than the PS3 store.

As far as visual novels go, I'd say this game is one of my favorites. If you're not familiar with visual novels, it's basically like reading a story with some choices sprinkled in. This game actually has puzzles in there, which are fun to play and are thematically involved with the story.

Speaking of the story, that's what's important with 999 -- and it's brilliant. I won't spoil it, but it starts off with a tense "Saw" like moment where the main character is abducted and put into a strange, life-threatening game along with 8 other people (thus making the "9 Persons" part of the title).

If there is one thing I have to insist on, it's that you play it on the Nintendo DS (or 3DS, as this game is compatible with the 3DS). I can't say why without ruining it, but BELIEVE when I say that the hardware it is played on is absolutely critical to getting the full impact of the story, and it's worth every moment of it. Other versions like the iOS port take out the puzzles and lose the full impact.

This is a game that can affect your sleep habits, as you get to revelations in the story and you just want to keep going to find out what happens next. Then you look up and 4 hours have passed.

One last thing -- when you get one ending, you're not done! Keep going until you get the "True" ending. It's not really "optional" as far as the story goes, it's actually kind of required. Don't worry -- it will all make sense in the end -- er, mostly.

They pretty much took the first game, fleshed-out the city, combat mechanics, skill system, story and writing, and made a great game. It's highly replayable, perfect for an Xbox 360 wireless controller on PC, and performs and looks even better than SOT.

I am not sure where people are getting that this game is "shorter" than SOT, it's easily 20 hours or more if you're completing side quests, crafting, and of course playing the challenge modes in the DLC to keep improving your character. There’s a lot of negative reviews about this game mainly towards the multiplayer.
I consider myself a COD multiplayer veteran and compared to the other COD games yes there’s a lot more camping here so you can’t run and gun as much on here. You really just need to adapt and change your play style. I’ll admit I hated it at first but then I got used to walking and checking corners more often now. I find myself having to increase my look sensitivity to check corners fast enough. The health is just like the original Modern Warfare where you’ll die within 2-3 hits so there shouldn’t be complaining there. I think people are just so used to Black Ops 3/4 where it literally takes half a clip to take someone out that they forgot how Modern Warfare was. Visually the game looks amazing. Played 1 hour of the campaign and it’s pretty good. It really feels like you’re there in the action. People also are upset that they paid $60 and they can’t play the campaign initially without an internet connection. To be fair when I picked up my preorder at GameStop I looked at the case and it specifically says on the bottom left corner “INTERNET REQUIRED”. I’m guessing people missed that hence the negative reviews. The weapon system is multiplayer is pretty cool. You can no longer have a million attachments without being penalized in some way. For example if you have a suppressor and a sight attachment, your aim down site (ads) speed will be much slower. The peeking/leaning over corners is a neat feature and it reminds me of Rainbow Six Siege. Ground War is pretty fun too. I like how you’re able to use vehicles now. This also reminds me of the Battlefield series. Again, if you’re used to playing the Black Ops series this may frustrate you at first, but give it some time to sink in. Rent it first if you’re hesitant it’s only $3 at redbox. I do that for games I’m unsure of. Every Call of Duty game that comes out will always have its complainers myself included at times. No one is ever satisfied. Of course this review is entirely my opinion and there will be others that feel the same and the opposite but I decided to give an honest review because it seems that there is just too much bashing on this game when it’s actually pretty good. Here’s a disclaimer “THIS GAME REQUIRES A LOT OF PATIENCE... A LOT” lol.

This is one of the greatest JRPGs of all time, I just wish the Switch had the power to do it more justice. This game would have been amazing at 1080p/60fps, but it's unfortunately more like 720p/30fps, although the frame rate is pretty solid and controller response is quite good for a 30fps game. On the plus side, there is so much to like- the upgraded graphics make this one of the Switch's best looking games (despite some blurry textures which are remnants from the Wii game). The remixed soundtrack makes the fantastic music even better, and the quality of life improvements are extremely welcome. Casual mode is less about being easier and more about saving time for me- battles can drag on otherwise, so this can be a real time saver. And you can switch between casual and normal whenever you like.
On the other hand, even though the graphics themselves look great, some dated animations are still there (they reuse the game walking animation at incorrect speeds in cut scenes and the result is very awkward looking), and the issue of hundreds of what I would consider unnecessary and often repetitive side quests (aka game padding) still persists. Also I played it with Japanese voices as I really didn't care for the British voices/localization, besides the fact it's only lip synced for Japanese. Regardless, Xenoblade is one of the greatest JRPGs ever made. Just be prepared for what you're getting into- it took me 150 hours to finish the main story, and about 15 hours to finish the extra chapter, although you could skip a lot and probably get through it much faster.

The last racing game I played was NFS Shift 2 and I loved that game. This game is very inferior to that game. The worst thing about the game is that it's dead boring as the developer intends to boost their microtransactions. Otherwise, it's missing conveniences that many other games offer. Just to be clear, I'm at driver level 40 in the game where currently only 3.5% of players have reached and have accumulated over 10,000,000 credits. I really only bought this game for the VGT cars. That's the only good thing I can say about it otherwise I would have bought Project Cars 2/3. This is just a short list of a few of my complaints/recommendations to the devs for GT7/GT8.

-The Lamborghini V12 Vision GT car was supposed to be in this game in Spring 2020, but they stripped it out (never released it like they said they would) and put it into GT7. False advertising to have ever said this game would ever include that car. I bought this game before that car was announced, so it's not like I bought this game for unmade content.
-Have an option to have the camera look into the corner as I drive towards it.
-There should be a free look option while driving in 3rd person. I'm a person who likes to admire his car from different angles during gameplay while driving on long straights. People argue that "it's not necessary for the gameplay", but I want it for the reason stated above. There's zero harm in making the right stick function like I want.
-The Home screen should allow you to do free look to admire your car and not have to exit from there and go through several more menus to reach a free look screen in the Livery Editor.
-Races always start with the over the hood camera position. I have to cycle through to get to the one I want with every race.
-Replays are in ultrawide.
-Arcade mode custom races need to allow me to save presets. EVERY SINGLE TIME I want to do a custom race I have to set every setting I want back to as I want.
-In Brand Central, you can't see if a car has beneficial upgrades available to it. Some cars can't be upgraded.
-Before a race, you select a car to drive, but they don't show you the stats of each car while in the pre-race car select screen.
-The game requires being online, connected to their servers. If you put your console into rest mode for a few hours with the game running, you'll have to restart the app because you can't hold a connection to their servers for long.
-If you change the paint of your car, to have it saved, you have to upload data which takes like 7sec.
-Paint finishes such as matte, chrome, or whatever aren't available unless you're lucky to see it in Brand Central. It will take several months for what you desire to come around and be available. A workaround that's a bit time consuming to go through is using decals that are stretched across the entirety of the car and having those set with the paint finish you want.
-Don't assume you can get all of the cars in the game by getting a free one every day. The free cars can be duplicates. I got this one car for free twice day after day. When you get your free car, they tease you with other cars. You're gambling your time for cars.
-Selling your cars comes at a loss. Adding to the grind for credits.
-Every single race is a rolling start. It takes time to reach the front, so each race is going to be long. The time to finish a race can be between 8min to 30min. If you fail a race, you'll spend another 30min doing the same >50mi race. As you continue losing in a race, your missing out earning creds. Once you achieve getting into first place through a race, the AI opponents become more difficult, meaning if you make a mistake, you risk losing the race and having wasted so much more time. Of course, they could have made every race a grid start and with three laps, but the devs want you to get exhausted, doing the same thing over, and over again. Games shouldn't have such repetition.
-The main menu shows you lots of random trivia to make you feel smart. I imagine they do that to make you feel more mature and want to think using your credit card to buy microtransactions makes you more of an adult.
-A female driver model would have been appreciated.
-Group B rallycross race 2. I have a Lancer Evo with street tires on asphalt and my car is sliding everywhere when going around a wide turn at 20mph. The car is behaving like I'm doing 50mph on dirt or something. This is a sim, right?
-They added a Toyota Tundra TRD Pro offroad truck to the game, but there's no rally venue you can enter it into to make good money. There's a venue dedicated to the Ford F150 Raptor with a couple races on dirt in there that include jumps, but Tundras aren't allowed. You can earn a few pennies driving that truck while in Arcade mode.
-Group 1 race 3. There's a corner in that race that's so sharp that even the AI opponents going as slow as possible like 5mph can't make the corner. I'm not mad about this point. It's actually kinda funny.

[[VIDEOID:6b3a8bdc371268c2808ee123f022d314]] I've been waiting for this game for for 10 years (since battlefront II came out in 2005). And I have mixed feelings after 1st day playing. I'm a star wars fan but not a fanboy. I'm a fan of the classic Battlefront II game on PS2 and while fun, I can't help thinking about all the features that were not included in this game that were in the last one. Also if you are looking for a BattleFIELD clone, look elsewhere. This game wasn't meant to be identical to Battlefield.

GRAPHICS/VISUALS: Best part of the game. Absolutely amazing. This game is beautifully rendered. From every desert stone on Jundland Wastes to the snow and ice of Hoth. Very detailed. I cannot speak highly enough about the visuals.

MULTIPLAYER: there are several multiplayer modes ranging from Hero battles, to aerial dogfights to 40 player deathmatch. Hero hunt and heroes vs villans are 2 modes where you have to take down jedi/sith like Luke and Vader. Aerial assault lets you pilot X-wings and tie fighters and dogfight. Walker Assault hsa the rebels attempting to destroy AT-AT walkers before they reach the base. There are only like 4 maps.....I wish there were more maps, but there is a new map coming December 8th. The game right now is all original trilogy, I haven't seen any heroes from ep 1,2,or 3. Battlefront II on PS2 had a ton of playable heroes from Yoda to General Greivous. In this game its just Han, Leia, Luke, Vader, Fett and Palpatine. The switching between 1st person and 3rd person is awesome, one of the best features in the game

SINGLE PLAYER: No Campaign! Single player is basically like an AI version of the multiplyer. They have a survival mode which is fun, you can do that with 1 or 2 players. I'm a fan of survival modes, loved call of duty zombies. This is like a star wars version, you just have to survive wave after wave of assaults.

DIFFERENCES FROM "STAR WARS: BATTLEFRONT II": The PS2 game was 32 v 32, while this game is 20 v 20. The 2005 game had 33 maps on 16 planets, this game has 4 planets. The 2005 game had space battles, this one has aerial assault but none in space. The 2005 game had 8 factions, this game has 2 (rebel vs imperial). 2005 game spanned prequel era and classic era, this game is just original trilogy. Last game had a campaign mode and a galactic conquest mode, this game does not. Its a shame that after 10 years and significantly better hardware, this game lacks many of the features that made the 2005 game great. this game is fun but as it stands now won't be the iconic great game that was Star Wars Battlefront II.

Bottom line is I like the game but I don't love it. Its not as hardcore as Call of Duty (which is perfect for me) its more casual. Its a fun game but it feels like EA held back alot for future DLC. The last star wars battlefront seemed alot more versatile and it came out in 2005. As it is right now it feels like it would get repetitive in about a month or 2, but then they'll come out with downloadable content and I'll probably pay for that too to get more maps weapons etc.

So I am a long time fan of the Final Fantasy series. I've played FF7, 8, 9, X, X-2, 13, FF Tactics, and both MMORPGS (FFXI and FFXIV). My first reaction playing this game was "this is not final fantasy". For the veteran final fantasy player this game takes some getting used to. Unlike previous games in the series, this game is modern (cell phones, cars, etc). The characters look more like a emo boy band than knights and mages. But after you play for a bit you get hooked just like any other Final Fantasy game.

GAMEPLAY: This game is an open world environment. For fans of the previous series you may be used to having to play through a linear progression until you unlock an airship allowing you to travel wherever you want. In this game it is mostly open world from the beginning. The world is large so running from one end to the other is out of the question, luckily you have a car! You can only drive on roads and in the beginning it seems very limiting. However once you travel from one city to the next you can generally "fast travel" there saving the time of actually driving for 5 minutes. Also chocobos can be utilized for travel through fields and deserts where the car cannot travel.

The fighting system is more action oriented rather than turn-based like most of the FF series. This felt very button mashing early on but I grew to enjoy it after learning the strategy around the battle system. Your party is fixed with Noctis (you) and his 3 friends/bodyguards. There is no swapping of party members. Each member of your party can equip a certain type of weapon and plays a certain type of role. These roles extend to non-fighting scenarios as well. For example Ignis is the "smart" one of the group, in battle he can analyze weakness of the enemy or heal and defend your party. Outside of battle he drives the car, and he cooks your meals (stat boosts). Gladius is the bodyguard and fighter, he deals the most damage in battle and outside of battle he sets up camp and helps you (Noctis) train. Prompto is the weakest in battle, uses a gun for long range attacks, outside of battle he is the group photographer (mostly useless).

Summons: I can't speak enough of the summons in this game. I was speechless the first time I summoned Titan. Every FF game has had pretty cool summons and well-done visual scenes. But the summons in this game are a whole different level. Unlike previous games you just can't summon whenever you want, the summons are so infinitely powerful that wouldn't be fair. The summons in this game are like Gods, so they kinda come out when they feel like it. Titan seems to come out when your party members are dead/dying and you are outside in the open. I think Ramuh comes out for long fights. Haven't gotten to Leviathan yet, that one is next for me.

VISUAL/GRAPHICS: Graphics in this game are amazing. The game has sort of a real-time mechanic. Every 2 minutes is an hour in gametime, so you see it change from day to night, sunrise to sunset. At nighttime much more powerful enemies come out so Ignis will refuse to drive and you are basically best off making camp or finding a hotel in an outpost. The backgrounds and landscapes all look amazing.

MUSIC: FF games have always had great music. However in this game I haven't had much time to pay attention to the FFXV music because when in the car you can play the soundtracks of every Final Fantasy game! So I spend alot of time listening to FFVII and FFXIII music.

STORY: biggest complaint I see from people is that the story is short. Since I had fair warning I am taking my time and free roaming/ side questing rather than going story quest full time. I am currently on chapter 5 and I believe there are 14 chapters total. So far the story is good and it has suspensful moments pretty early on. Also of note is that there is an anime (FFXV brotherhood) and a movie (FFXV Kingsglaive) that take place concurrently with the story of this game that gives more backstory to the world. EDIT: I am on chapter 7 no and these chapters are blazing by really fast. EDIT: So now on Chapter 13 and there are only 14 chapters. This game (storyline wise) is very short. Progressing past chapter 8 seems to be a point of no return and you can no longer roam freely on the world map (which makes game blaze by even faster since you can't get distracted by sidequests). I have to knock off a star for the shortness of the story. The story so far is good but the shortness of it leaves it far below the gold standard that games like FFVII have set. Releasing Kingsglaive and Brotherhood (movie and anime set in same world) does not excuse shortening the story of the actual game.

I bought this Deluxe Edition digitally so I could play Modern Warfare Remastered early. Let me tell you, it's not how I remembered it. The game was king by 2007 standards but in 2016 it has not aged gracefully. It has one core gameplay loop - shoot stuff, shoot incoming waves of enemies. The shooting incoming hordes of bad guys was big last generation. It was a staple in Uncharted, Gears of War, where it felt like you killed 100 guys and they just kept coming still. Modern Warfare Remastered is built on this and it's not nearly as fun as it was in 2007, so prepare to have your nostalgia goggles broken a bit.

The Remastered graphics are also decent but not that good. This game still looks more last gen than current, like they copied and pasted the PS3 version assets, applied bright lighting, less grainy textures and depth of field and called it a day. Some assets, like trees, look to be the same PS3 assets with no change at all. It's clear here that Modern Warfare Remastered was never intended to be the star this holiday season, and it will probably be forgotten about once everyone gets their nostalgia fix.

The idea behind a Life is Strange prequel with Chloe at center stage really didn't convince me at first, but I loved the original and I just had to dive into this one as soon as the game released for physical. Chloe was angst-y and, if I'm being blunt, a bit of an ass in the first game; although, she did have her moments and was an overall good to decent character. I really felt like Max helped draw out these better qualities from her. That explains much of the skepticism. Happy to say that the game definitely exceeded expectations, and added so much more depth to Chloe's character in explaining why she was the way she was in the original. I wasn't totally convinced with Rhianna DeVries as Chloe initially, but a certain scene in a junkyard sold me on the new voice as the actress nailed this sort of desperate vulnerability. Rachel becomes much more than the face on a poster she is in the first game, and becomes this endearing but unhinged character. Subplots and side characters were very well done, and I particularly enjoyed the dynamic between Mikey, Steph and Drew. Soundtrack really nailed the atmosphere and mood here, which is a bit like the first game's but a bit more abrasive and "punk".

Limited Edition includes a soundtrack album and a mini art book, both of which are decent but don't expect anything elaborate. The art book isn't very in-depth, with some outfit concepts and scenery. Really nothing to write home about. Album's worth the money if you're into that. It's really a collector's thing, so for an extra $10 ain't bad. Base game is a satisfying experience by itself.

The annual Call of Dury season is upon us as we return to the Second World War or the current political climate loosely inspired by WWII. Vanguard only exists to put WW2 weapons in Warzone. You know it, I know it the game itself is like 2019’s Modern Warfare. The graphics are like MW2019, so it looks better than Cold War graphically. With 20 maps at launch and six seasons of multiplayer planned, and even an Attack on Titan crossover planned. The campaign is a woke Michael Bay movie that most of you aren’t even going to play. It’s pretty mid and short, not one of Call of Duty’s best campaigns. Finally, zombies, it’s barebones and needs content.

Honestly, the game was better than I expected. After playing the beta, I was sure the game was heading for a flop. They manage to ship the game in a better state than Battlefield 2042. All things considered, for a filler entry, you can’t go wrong with this season's Call of Duty as it’s fun, not going to lie.

Battlefield 2042 is what happens when EA rushes the game and chases the latest trends—abandoning Battlefield V after ruining that game with a series of blunders. We get Battlefield 2077 at an unfinished state unless you're a YouTuber on EA’s payroll. You miraculously get a bugless experience.

Battlefield 2042 removes classes for operators removing a core part of the experience so you can spend that sweet money on new operators and cosmetics when they inevitably drop once they fix the game in six months. Now everyone looks the same and does their own thing, just like Call of Duty Warzone, only worse as the game is buggy, the hit detection is all over the place. All the maps are too big, even with 120 players. Suppose you don't get a vehicle; well, good luck. Hazard Zone, the Battle Royale-inspired mode, is not good. It's the only mode where Operators fit, but without any friends, it's dreadful.

The best mode is the Battlefield portal. A game mode that remasters classic battlefield games and gives the community a bunch of options and returns the battlefield to its roots of class-based gameplay. It also has more weapons than the base Battlefield 2042. A lot of potential here, and if DICE updates it with more maps and Battlefield games, we got the crown jewel of Battlefield 2042. It ready saves the game from being an absolute disaster.

Battlefield 2042 is the Battlefield for the Zoomer Generation. Chasing trends that made Call of Duty and Rainbow 6 Siege lots of money. Of course, EA wasn’t going to ignore that, and it’s not the worse thing ever; franchises got to evolve; operators are the future of multiplayer games. It is what it is. Fortnite changed the industry. However, this game takes steps back and frankly feels like a downgrade from Battlefield 4. I'm sure in 6 months, they'll iron out most technical issues and add more weapons and maps. But you can also buy it in 6 months when it’s not $70 and a better game.

Everything or Nothing changes the formula from the previous 007 games and goes from being a first person shooting like experience to a 3rd person experience. It's not a bad idea on paper but sadly this game suffers from bad design in execution.

I'll start with the good points. This game has good visual quality. The Gamecube version isn't as stunning to see as the Xbox version which I suspect is due to the smaller data storage of the discs it uses but all the content manages to be here. The voice acting is done by the cast of the movies and all the facial models are as well. The gadgets are interesting and unique.

Now for the bad. The gameplay is pretty terrible, most notably the 3rd person perspective levels when you're actually running around and not driving a car, helicopter or whatnot. This game's design falls somewhere between stealth and action. The problem is the controls are designed to promote stealth while the action you encounter will punish you for trying to be stealthy. It's kind of hard to explain but imagine 5 enemies running toward you all firing their weapons. You're naturally going to want to pull out your weapon, take aim and strafe behind a wall for cover while returning fire. Here's the real kicker, you CANNOT aim your weapon unless you've locked onto an enemy. There is no free aiming in this game unless you have a sniper rifle that you won't get into much later in the game. And it doesn't really help either because the aiming speed of the rifle is way way too slow. You'll never be able to pick off a couple enemies before they riddle you with bullets.

Don't get me wrong, it's playable, it's beatable but the big problem is it is not fun. I almost want to laugh because I know that if I read this review I would think "Oh, you just didn't play it right"...No, it really is badly designed for the majority of it. I picked it up for $5 used and I'm glad I didn't pay more. I'm going to complete all there is to it, get the platinum medals and such, and then I am never ever going to play this game again, guaranteed. Do yourself a favor, if you're itching for a Bond game, pick up Agent Under Fire, Nightfire, the N64's GoldenEye, anything but this. I'm being generous giving it 2 stars because the gadgets are cool.

Quick note, this refers to the Gamecube version. Agent Under Fire is one of the best of the 007 games you can find right next to the follow up 007: Nightfire. It's a first person shooter game with some mission elements requiring you to use gadgets to do such things like hack a computer or chase down and disable a vehicle.

Gameplay wise I'm really fond of how everything is executed. It never feels like the controls or gameplay is designed poorly although I did find myself using the option 3 control scheme instead of the default controls. As for the music and voice work, it's all done very well.

The only blemish this game has are the occasional pre rendered cutscenes. I'm not even sure why there's pre rendered cutscenes in this game because there are plenty of real time cutscenes that look great. The pre rendered ones however are LAUGHABLY bad, like I just can't believe they would've thought they were ok to do. I've seen 240p Youtube videos that would put the pre rendered cutscenes to shame in terms of video quality, it's so laughably bad. Luckily, there's not that many, most cutscenes aren't pre rendered.

Great game, this one and 007: Nightfire are must haves in my book.

Sometimes there's really not a lot to say about a product: it's nothing fancy but it excels at what it set out to do. The Amazon Basics dock can charge four Joy-cons at a time. It doesn't care which side (left or right) goes in which port, it holds them securely but not so tightly it's a pain to get them out, and it charges them at a rapid clip. If only everything executed this well.

Look, I like things that just *work.* The PowerA charging station just *works* and I love it for that.

First off, it's officially licensed by Sony, so it works perfectly with the stock controllers right our of the box with no fiddling.

The charger itself is fairly light but weighted toward the bottom. This, combined with the weight of the controller's "wings," bring the center of gravity fairly low, lending it a good degree of stability; it survives a decent knock without the controller coming off.

There are no indicator lights on the charger itself, but the PS5 controller itself will give you a brief slow orange flash to let you know it's charging. This is a blessing for those of us who like our gaming spaces dark and free of random blinking LEDs.

Overall, it's a well-designed product that does exactly what it's supposed to at a very reasonable price point.

And Contracts, which remade some levels from the first game and gave the series a dark spin... And now we arrive at this: The much anticipated Hitman Blood Money. It is quite impressive, so we'll start with the good first. The graphics are amazing, especially for PS2. Everything looks rich and detailed and runs smoothly. Also, The missions are much more verried, huge and fun to explore. The new "accident" system is fun, but in my opinion makes the game easier (civilians killed in an accident or bodies found from the result of an accident don't count off of your rating for a level...) There are so many ways to earn a Silent Assassin rating on a level, the possibilities are endless, which means replay for this title is through the roof. A certian number of weapons can be customized as well, which is a very nice touch and a welcome addition to the series.

Now, the not-so-good stuff... Well, a few of the levels aren't quite as enjoyable as the others. Hitman 2 suffered from this problem greatly, but it could afford to, seeing as it had a whopping 20 levels. Whith Blood Money sporting only 12 real missions, it can't afford to have 2 or 3 that are sub par. Also, just like the past titles, this one has a few levels that will instantly stand out as classics. The Murder of Crows will be a favorite for any aspiring Mass Murderer, and one or two other levels specificly stand out above the rest. The wepon selection is rather limited from past games (which is, in my opinion, nothing to complain about. All the wepons are now varied and have their own look and feel, unlike past titles). Also, only a limited number of weapons can be upgraded. Agent 47 starts with a Sp12 shotgun, His signiture .45s, the Wa2000 sniper rifle, M4 assault rifle and a submachine gun at his hide out. These 5 weapons are the only ones that can be customized, meaning these will be the only 5 weapons you ever use unless you are experimenting with others from your quickly amassed collection. The levels are open ended, with many ways to make a hit and get away clean, but in my opinion, this lowers the difficulty significantly. Also included is the inclusion of "natority". This was a nifty gimmick, but in the end, that's all it is. Play sloppy and you get noticed by witnisses, etc. and future missions become harder, as cops start to recognize you, based on descriptions from witnisses and being caught on camera. Natority can be getten rid of quickly by bribing witnisses, or you can get rid of it entirely and for free by getting a better rank on missions you did sloppy on (which isn't hard). Also, while enemy AI has been beefed up and is FAR more realistic and believable than before, it falls to pieces in a firefight. While sneaking around, enemies behave well, and NPCs believably, but when things go wrong and a fire fight breaks out, innocents run for cover, while guards and police usually stand in one spot and shoot at you till their clip is empty. No hiding behind corners, or even ducking... just standing still shooting, reload, repeat. This is a shame, but the challenge comes not from killing all the bad guys as much as it does making a clean get-away. In conclusion, Blood Money is far more streamlind and well played out than Contracts or even HM2. The Graphics are great, the new features are a welcome addition, but are being overplayed and over hyped in my opinion. Short and sweet, this is the hitman you've come to know and love, and has far fewer flaws than some other games in the series. It features a few great levels, one or two bad ones and a strong showing of good ones. It is well rounded, with improved AI, a decent selection of weapons and very open ended levels. Although a little too easy in my opinion, I can say that as day's go by and I play more, this is becoming my favorite Hitman, little by little.

The Fallen Order is a large scale single-player action-adventure game that was developed by Respawn Entertainment and published by EA. This game is unlike most titles published under the EA trade mark, and features a lengthy development time with no interference from EA. This time around, EA has stayed entirely hands off, and has allowed Respawn Entertainment all of the time and money necessary in order to create such a massive and well polished adventure. Players that are however looking to play with friends may be disappointed and find there is no multiplayer, but the flip side of the coin is that players get a well polished single player game that was able to receive the teams undivided attention.

There are absolutely no lootboxes or microtransactions found in the game, and comes fully loaded with goodies we now take for granted these days and mostly end up needing to pay for. There is lightsaber customization, offering a host of different colors, as well as being able to change the emitter, switch, sleeve and material. The game comes with 23 Poncho outfits with 5 different patterns, 15 BD-1 alternate colors and 13 for the Mantis. The player must however find these items hidden throughout the worlds intricate level design. Fallen Order is massive and features a few different planets with each having its own looks, enemies and lore, and packs a meaty campaign with a solid 18-30 hours depending on your play style, search for secrets and difficulty settings. The game is what I would call "wide linear". I don't want to spoil how many planets there are, but players are free to play a few of them in their own order, and can always go back to the ship and travel to any previous location.

The levels are massive and intelligently designed, packed with secret items and hidden chambers around every corner. As players gain more powers, they will often find themselves wanting to return to locations in order to reach areas that was once out of reach. The gameplay is packed with lots variety. There are bosses, unlockable powers, hidden items and lore, lots of platforming, tomb raiding, swimming, large worlds to explore and puzzles to solve. The levels always have a "metroidvania" design, with more than one way to traverse and shortcuts that are often found and unlocked for players that wish to return. Players will also find that the story is well done and aims to keep the player fully engaged from start to finish. The level of quality and polish here is amazing.

The combat can be very challenging and can often feel like Sekiro in the way it controls. The player must learn to master the defensive approach and adapt to enemy patterns and adjust strategies fluently. When killed in combat, the enemy that takes you down will grab the players gained experience, but returning to gain a single blow will restore the experience. Jedi Master is the 3rd difficulty setting and can be tough enough, offering an equal balance of parry time, incoming damage and enemy aggression. Jedi Grandmaster on the other hand is an entirely different beast, with enemies doing 50% more damage, 50% more aggressive, and the parry time is around 50% faster. The upgrade system is also well done and makes the player feel like a real Jedi Knight. Earning skill points takes time and must be earned, as the player must find secrets and defeat some very strong enemies along the way in order to get the most of these skill points.

The skill tree is broken into three categories, Force, Lightsaber and Survival. There is a true feel of accomplishment and player progression, as skills are gradually unlocked and you start to become a powerful hero. Throughout your journey, BD-1 will also collect much needed skills in order to help aid the player. Combat can require pinpoint accuracy and feel demanding at times, and the skills feel necessary in shaping you into the Jedi one should be. Nothing is to excessively complex, just simple player observation and being able to slow down and take in whats happening around them. When doing so, players will find there is a great amount of variety to the formula, and just when you think you have seen it all, they toss a double-bladed Lightsaber into the mix. The HUD is also worth mentioning, there is no screen clutter, just a small health bar placed on the bottom left of the screen. There is also a generous amount of game settings. Players can fully edit the controls, scale subtitle size, set chromatic aberration, film grain, camera shake, motion blur, multiple audio outputs and more.

Final Verdict:

We are slowly starting to see the return of well polished single player games, as many studios are starting to wake up and realize its not always about online games. This is a game that has exceeded my expectations and packs one of the best single player adventures on the market. Don't let the EA trade mark fool you this time around, Fallen Order is well worth the price of admission. I didn't cover any story aspects in hopes of avoiding spoilers, but players can rest assure that Star Wars fans are in for a ride, as everything shows homage to the tone and lore of the Star Wars universe. Even if your not into Star Wars, I would say its more than worth a try.

Shenmue is a game I am no stranger to. I was a big fan of the Dreamcast and the original Shenmue was part of my collection, so it was no surprise when the second game came around it also became part of my collection. Looking back into the past, I find most of those memories are tied to nostalgia. It was once a game that I had a blast playing, but it's incipient that in the passing of 2 decades times have changed. Shenmue started development in 1993 and was originally intended to be a Sega Saturn game. After 6 years of development, it finally dropped in 1999 for the Dreamcast. Shenmue was the most expensive video game ever developed at that time, and said to have cost around 40-70 million. From a narrative, gameplay and graphical perspective, it was unparalleled and far ahead of its time. True competition didn't arrive to the table until the release of Yakuza for the PlayStation 2 during the end of 2005 in Japan, but it was actually 2006 for the release outside of Japan.

With such advancements, including the recent release of Judgement, the conception of Shenmue 3 can feel very dated, as newer games have perfected and polished a formula that was once an exclusive formula of the Shenmue series. This is however a good and bad thing. If you change to much, it feels nothing like the originals and you disrupt the core fan base, but if you change to little it feels dated and out of sync. This is a game that doesn't try to cater to a newer crowd and has only one goal in mind. That goal is replicating the presentation of the previous games, and its simply remarkable how they managed to capture the charm, visual style and sound of the original games. Shenmue 3 is a game that follows the motto "if its not broke don't fix it". In many ways, it faces the same shortcomings as Duke Nukem Forever. For many new to the series, it seemed like a horribly low budget and poorly crafted game, but in reality, it was more of the same. The problem it faced was that it paid its debut years after it was ever expected, and the game faced a newer generation of people that got stuck with an old formula that showed its age. As a result, the finished product felt extremely dated by time it ever saw the light of day.

Shenmue 3 did enter a period of development over a decade ago, but do to the failure of Shenmue City, it left funds dried up, so the project got pulled in 2011. Kickstarter was necessary for the new development of Shenmue 3 to begin, but the campaign needed to raise no less than 10 million, and ended up raising around 7 million from around 80,000 supporters. It ended up being to small for a high-profile game, but Sony and Deep Silver ended up providing further backing. The truth is that Shenmue has always been a niche series and it's not a game that will suit everyone's needs. Most of your love for the game will originate from nostalgia, and being able to pick back up from a story that never received the leisure of closure. I'm not ashamed to say that with such a substantial passing of time, there are games that do excel in many regards over the delivered product. However, there is still a part of me that grew up with the original games, and once such a poignant seed had been planted, it is hard to forget the memories one carries with them over the years.

Even with funds being raised from crowdfunding, the game is still very large and even more so than the previous games, and it's packed with tons of optional side content and mini-games. Some of the mini-games from Shenmue 1 and 2 make a return, and many new ones have been added for the first time in the series. The menu also features a nicely done digest movie, and it does a great job in covering the story of the first 2 games. The game features 4 difficulty settings and has a well rounded balance for players of all kinds. The combat system has also received an overhaul for the better, and features a wide range of moves that offer a great amount of user flexibility. There are plenty of locations for training, as well as a wide host of characters standing by in order to aid the player in the development of skills. The world is packed full of collectibles ranging from skill books, foods, herbs, different outfits and more. Shenmue 3 is without hesitation, a worthy installment of the series, packed with mini games, a progressive fighting system, a well crafted world inhabited with memorable characters, and a bountiful story that takes hold and never lets go.

Final Verdict:

I would highly recommend this game to any hardcore fan of the series, as the new installment doesn't deviate from the original roots. If you have never played Shenmue, start with the first 2 installments, because the digest movie is not the same as experiencing the real thing. Back at the turn of the millennium, Shenmue was the pinnacle of highly immersive gaming and told an epic tale. It also featured a revolutionary day and night system and weather system that had never been attempted before, and individual NPCs would also go about their own daily routines. It felt like you weren't playing a game called Shenmue, but was actually participating in the life of Ryo Hazuki. Are the overall controls, graphics, and production values more advanced then other competition found on today's market? The answer is no. Does the overall game still feature the original magic that was there from the beginning, and seek to bring levity and understanding to an unfinished journey? The answer is most definitely yes. My respects to those who showed backing and support, and my best regards to Deep Silver, Sony Entertainment, and co-producer Shibuya Productions, as everyone played a substantial role in helping Yu Suzuki make the impossible possible.

In any case, it is a fun game. Especially if you have 6 hours at a time to kill, like I do.

Ah, the Prince of Persia series--a saga with which I have held a love/hate relationship for the past twenty years. I've played the original, the SNES versions, the horrific Prince of Persia 3D--as well as the Prince's latest forays, the Sands of Time and the Warrior Within.

So, what exactly is the Two Thrones? It's the conclusion of the Prince of Persia trilogy started by Sands of Time and Warrior Within. I suppose, logically, the story makes sense; it is a return to the visual splendor and level structure that made the Sands of Time such a joy to play, and also offers the combat system and some of the darker overtones of the Warrior Within.

But I am left with the impression that Ubisoft was responding to the critism that Warrior Within received with the Two Thrones. Consequently, some of the aspects that worked well with the Warrior Within have been simplified.

Combat is the best example of this. One thing I liked about Warrior Within is that there was the distinct possibily of running into evil sand creatures while negotiating obstacles. Not so with the Two Thrones; in instead returns to the "obstacle-enemy-obstacle" system that the Sands of Time used.

The story is another example of Ubisoft reacting to "The Warrior Within." Although Warrior Within sold better than its predecessor, it received critisim for essentially destroying the story established by the Sands of Time. And so Ubisoft does it again; by consciously attempting to return the series to its roots, most of the story elements offered by the Warrior Within are ripped out and given only a cursory transition in the narrative. I'd like it if Ubisoft could form a more coherent story. Story gets 3/5 stars.

Well; now I've got the story problems out of the way, so let's take a look at the technical aspects of the game, shall we?

Graphics: Eye candy. The graphics are very good, but my only complaint is that they sometimes look "washed out," due to the lighting effects of the sun. 4/5.

Sound: Much better than the Warrior Within. The Prince seems to have got his original voice actor back, and the voice acting is well-done. 5/5.

Design: The obstacles are very well thought-out, but my only complaint is that they're pretty straight forward. Enter room, swing from poles, run cross wall, etc. Come on, Ubisoft; isn't there more than one way to skin a cat?

A very big complaint I have about the design is that some of it just doesn't make sense--most notably, the diagonal jumps that are placed along walls. Why are they there? Surely the building architects didn't put them there for the explicit purpose of some wall-bounding, pole swinging half-naked nutjob to use. But yet, there they are, for some nonsensical reason. What I loved about the Sands of Time and the Warrior Within is that the Prince worked WITHIN the enivronment to get where he needs to go; here, it seems like Ubisoft constructed the environments AROUND the Prince, which is disappointing. 2/5.

Gameplay: more than anything, this is where the game suffers. The combat seems stripped down from the "Warrior Within;" seriously, all you really have to do to beat most enemies is keep bounding over their heads. The formula goes like this:

1.) Find enemy

2.) Bound over its head, score two strikes.

3.) Bound over its head, have attack blocked.

4.) Bound over its head, score two strikes.

5.) Repeat.

Combat can be frustrating, especially since the game throws a large host of button-mashing combos at you early in the game and expects you to remember them. Fortunately, you can access these combos at any time on the pause menu, but really . . . who among us racks their brain trying to remember "Triangle Triangle Square Square Square Triangle" while in the middle of a boss battle?

But the biggest complaint I've got is simple game issues. Yesterday, I went to run up a wall and fell right through it. The Prince pulled a ghost number, falling to his demise because he clipped right through a stone wall. And this morning, my game froze--extremely frustrating after twenty minutes of pole swinging, guard dodging, and switch-pulling.

So, is the Two Thrones a worthy addition to the Prince of Persia saga? Yes, it is. It just isn't the best.

The Castlevania series has undergone its fair share of criticism; i.e., the Metroid-style structure has been done to death, and there simply aren't enough innovations to distinguish the games from each other. The 3D games have been particularly aligned, with poor level structure being the widest complaint.

Portrait of Ruin was Konami's answer to those complaints. While the design of the game has been restructured, the overall execution is somewhat lacking.

For example, the game's protagonists, Jonathan Morris and Charlotte Aulin, must use paintings, much in the style of Super Mario 64, to enter new worlds. Here's where part of the problem lies--there are only five distinct levels (Dracula's Castle, a city overrun with monsters, a dark forest, Egypt, and a twisted circus sideshow.) You can find restructured and more difficult versions of these levels later on in the game, but the overall lack of diversity is disappointing. Instead of offering different versions of the same levels, Konami could have delved into Castlevania's 20-year history to deliver us mountain ranges, or sleepy villages, or haunted docks, or sunken ruins . . . the list goes on, and its rather aggravating to find such a lack of effort in this title.

However, the dual-hero system works well for the game. Sadly, there aren't very many puzzles in which you must rely on your partner--yes, there is a segment in which the two characters ride motorcycles and the player must shift between the two to clear the course--but events like these are few and far between. Most often, the only reason you'll switch to Charlotte is to turn into a frog or an owl, or to cast a specific spell. You'll spend the other 90% of the time as Jonathan.

The difficulty is also somewhat skewed. Most enemies can be ripped through quickly and easily, but boss battles can be intensely difficult, with bosses often using attacks that can drain as much as 200 hit points. Attention to patterns and a plentiful supply of potions are necessary to win the day, and while its refreshing to have boss battles reminiscent of the old-school 8-bit Castlevanias, players who entered the series with Symphony of the Night are in for a rude awakening.

However, the story is top-notch, and follows roughly thirty years after the events of Castlevania: Bloodlines for the Sega Genesis. The characters are well-written, and the player will become genuinely intrigued by their stories and their pasts.

Sounds, as usual, are one of the highlights for the game. The voice-acting is present, but generally minimal, and the melodies and sound effects continue to be haunting.

Enemy design is also one of the game's highest points. The sprites are well-animated, and, in many portions of the game, comical. For example, the Persephone enemy shuffles back and forth with a vacuum cleaner; if Jonathan gets too close, he'll be sucked backwards and get his bottom lodged in the end of the appliance. Charlotte, conversely, will be momentarily inconvenienced as she struggles to prevent her skirt from being blown up. One boss enemy can also seduce Jonathan with one of her attacks, causing him to attack Charlotte.

In conclusion, Portrait of Ruin is a game that belongs in every Castlevania fan's library. It's just not particularly memorable.

So I finally finished the game. It took me 152 hours spread across 4 months but I did it. You're definitely getting your money's worth in terms of longevity and it was a genuinely fun experience.

However I did have some gripes, the first being the romance options for the two playable characters - Alexios and Kassandra. My Kassandra was heterosexual, but it felt like I was being forced to either play as a straight Alexios or a gay Kassandra. Most of the romanceable characters were attractive, strong females but the five male options I was able to find were...not great. One seemed nice until he casually asked to help kill his mother, one had erectile dysfunction, one was a complete a-hole and another seemed willing to have sex with anything with a pulse, including a goat...heck I'm not sure having a pulse was even required. There's even an instance where a very likable female character is killed by your hands if you don't pursue a romantic relationship with her (RIP Roxana). On the topic of romance, I was also a bit disappointed by the lack of nudity considering the ancient Greek setting. You know...for immersion and stuff.

Another personal gripe is that Odyssey is an Assassin's Creed game, something that I think limits it creatively. Some of my favorite moments in Odyssey involved fighting mythical creatures like the Minotaur and Medusa. But these were too sparse, likely attributed to the game's adherence to the AC lore. Sailing around on the Adrestia would be a lot more exciting if at any moment you could be attacked by a giant sea serpent or the Kraken or even Cthulhu. I wish Odyssey was a new IP similar to the older God of War or Prince of Persia games, where you encounter more supernatural enemies.

That said the game was fantastic. The story was great, though in my opinion the present day stuff is still ruined thanks to AC3. The game was also not as grindy as many claimed, so long as you view it as an rpg and not an action/adventure/stealth like past AC games. There's one final detail I noticed and I'd like to mention. If the character happens to be walking through a field of wheat, they will gently brush their hand along the top of the wheat plants a la Gladiator. I absolutely love small animation details like this. Well done Ubisoft.

The Good.
Beautiful graphics, solid gameplay and great longevity. I enjoyed most of the 244 hours I played and all with a surprising lack of bugs. Also I personally love the injection of Metal Gear Solid into The Division and would like to see it carried even further.

The Bad.
The story and characters are horribly bland. Despite the name, you're not getting a gripping espionage thriller worthy of Tom Clancy here.

The Ugly.
Character customization sucks. You're limited to a handful of slightly tweakable faces that you cannot re-design later without starting a new campaign. There are a few boring hairstyles and a basic body type for male and female stuck in a ridiculous posture that makes you look like you're siting on an invisible pony. Apparel is a particular disappointment and the primary reason I got bored with the game due to how samey they are. No reason to continue playing beyond collecting more gear with random numbers attached to them, most of which you'll sell for in-game money you can't spend on anything useful thanks to premium currency.
