Though I have a PS4 and play many games on it, I dislike that it isn't backwards compatible with previous generations and have been buying more games (both old and new) on Steam, since it seems backwards compatibility isn't as much of an issue on Steam. When I ordered a Steam Link last fall to play the games I was buying on my TV, I initially tried using one of my PS4 controllers. I only have two, and normally I am charging one while using the other with my PS4, and I found it difficult to make one of the PS4 controllers connect to both the Steam Link and the PS4 - the PS button would often either turn both on or it would turn the wrong one on, and I would have to disconnect it from the other one and make sure it was connected to the one I wanted to use, and it was very time consuming. Thus, I decided I needed a dedicated controller for the Steam Link, and my options were to either go with this Steam Controller or to get another PS4 controller. When just connecting normally to Steam games, even, many of the games require the PS4 controller to be configured correctly, and it is difficult and un-intuitive to figure out how to configure the PS4 controller and the game will not work if it is not correctly configured. Given this issue and the fact that used Steam controllers tend to be cheaper than used PS4 controllers, I decided to get the Steam controller for use with my new Steam Link. It has worked out very well so far. It connects to the Steam Link and can be used to turn the Steam Link on by pressing the Steam button on the controller, just like the PS4 is turned on by pressing the PS button on the PS4 controllers. Also, the Steam controller works immediately with every Steam game, with no need for confusing configuration beforehand. The only confusing thing that sometimes happens is that games will frequently give keyboard and mouse instructions, and it is not always obvious how that is laid out on the Steam controller (for example, I have been playing Final Fantasy VII recently and it said to press [OK] to jump, and I had to spend a few minutes figuring out which button that was - eventually I figured out that it corresponded to B and I also had to be positioned correctly in the game). Also, being used to a PS4 controller's layout, I found the Steam controller's layout initially awkward and un-intuitive, but the more I use it the more I grow to like it and appreciate the layout. It essentially tries to combine a regular controller with a mouse, and it does so rather effectively. On the controller side, it has the menu buttons in the center, the four action buttons on the right, and then it gives you a joystick and direction buttons on the left. The only thing it lacks from my PS4 controller, then, is a second joystick, but otherwise it is exactly like a PS4 controller in terms of having all the same features. It even has the right and left buttons on top. These top buttons also serve a dual purpose - they are essentially used as the two buttons on a mouse when the controller is meant to act more like a mouse (such as in menu screens when loading a game). These work well as mouse button replacements. It attempts to recreate moving your mouse around via the large black circle on the right. While the circle on the left has a shallow inlay of direction buttons and is meant to act as a direction pad, the right circle is completely smooth and it is meant for you to move your thumb or finger across to move a mouse cursor around. This doesn't do as great of a job mimicking moving a mouse around as the rest of the controller does in mimicking a regular game controller, but I don't see how one could do better in implementing mouse functionality in a controller. Overall, while awkward at first, the Steam controller becomes more intuitive with increased use and I have grown to appreciate how it is a combination of a regular game controller and a mouse. The only negative I have for this controller is that it takes two AA batteries instead of having rechargeable batteries like the PS4 controllers. While I have purchased a set of rechargeable AA batteries and can just take them out and recharge them when needed (and the batteries seem to last a while, at least a few weeks of playing a couple hours a day), I would still prefer if there was built-in rechargeable batteries in the controller, so I could just plug it into my computer or a wall outlet and charge it when it is low on batteries just like I do with my PS4 controllers. I think that is the biggest criticism of this controller, and it only slightly makes using it less convenient. Overall, I think this is a great controller and highly recommend it if you use Steam a lot and have a Steam Link or another Steam console. It is definitely a rather unique and versatile controller, and it pairs better with Steam than other non-Steam controllers, even quality controllers from a brand like Sony. I hope this helps you enjoy your Steam games!

Though I have a PS4 and play many games on it, I have been purchasing many of my old games on Steam as well as newer games, since there seems to be less backwards compatibility issues on PC than on the PS4. Since I prefer playing on my TV than on my laptop, I ordered this Steam Link last fall when it was on sale in order to have easier access for playing all of my new Steam games on the screen I prefer. This seems to do an excellent job streaming games to the TV. I merely open Steam on my PC, then I turn on the device with my Steam controller and navigate to my connected PCs and choose my laptop (the only one currently out there) from the list, and it connects and I can play my Steam games through it. The most graphics-intensive game I have played is Grand Theft Auto V, and it seemed to work well for the most part. There were some instances where it lagged, but it was difficult to decide whether it was due to the Steam Link or due to my PC lagging - I think often it was due to my PC, which while specced for gaming, is definitely on the cheaper end of gaming computers. It was a few months ago when I was playing Grand Theft Auto V frequently on the Steam Link, and I noticed then that sometimes it would be unable to find my computer even though I had Steam running, and sometimes I would have to either re-start Steam, the Steam Link, or sometimes I just re-started my computer entirely, but it generally connected after re-starting one of them. After taking a break to play some PS4 games, I have recently started playing Final Fantasy VII over the Steam Link, and I have not found any issues connecting to my computer as long as I have Steam already open, so I'm not sure if there was an update or anything but that seems to be much less of an issue in my recent playing than there was a couple months ago. Also, I have experienced essentially zero lag when playing Final Fantasy VII, which is a much less graphics-intensive game than Grand Theft Auto V. Overall, I think this is an amazing streaming device for your Steam games, especially if you can get it on sale for $10 on a Steam sale as I did. It seems to connect well with little lag, especially on games that aren't very graphics-intensive. If you prefer sitting on your couch and playing games on your TV instead of at your desk, then this Steam Link is a great way to get your Steam games onto your TV screen, and costs much less than purchasing a separate Steam console if you already have a gaming computer. I highly recommend this if you have a Steam library!

Hopefully (but unlikely) Sega will release a mini version of the Master System, Sega CD, and Dreamcast. But the Saturn can burn! Fortunately for me, I still have all of my old consoles (Saturn included.)

It's the story of two brothers in search for a cure for their ailing father. The language is purely fictitious and yet as a gamer, you completely understand the story that's being foretold.

Initially, the controls were hard to manage, but then you get used to it. The left analog stick controls the big brother and the right stick controls the younger brother. Aside from traversing the land, I usually ended up only controlling one brother at a time to do certain tasks. So, in other words, don't let the controls put you off from playing this game. Once you start playing, you will want to continue until the very end. It's a short game (around 4 hours - depending on your play style), but well worth playing. You will think about it long after you've finished it. The puzzles are doable, the atmosphere is wonderful, and the soundtrack is exquisite. I liked that you can customize the appearance of your hostess girls and that's how they look when you go on disco dates. Karaoke, while not my thing, was a thing to see. So many diversions, and it never felt like the side stuff hurt the pace of the main story. No Ciri, Yen, Triss, etc... depth of romance. Koi-koi is no japanese gwent. Not enough messed up shenanigans. Although it got pretty damn close. I mean this wasn't full-on Battle Royale, it was more like Red Cliff, but if the future Yakuza games can hit this type of content and quality, then I'm all-in.

"Senran Kagura X Persona" is the holy grail of game design.

While NOA2 doesn't nearly get there (it's more SK than P4), it's a step in the ideal direction. Just needs more of the good stuff.

25 hours to beat, I jumped into New Game + right away, but decided to put it back on the shelf until the time limit is patched out. The time limit just destroys the pleasure of the grind. So I'm back into Peach Beach Splash.

If Sony/Koei Tecmo ever get their act together, I expect I'll put 75-100 hours into this with a few more ng+ runs.

Swimsuits! is japanese game aesthetic at it's finest. Like the victoria secrets fashion show has to save the world. It works really well with the busty lesbian vampire opera theme. The only knock is the blonde girl has a lame swimsuit. Such potential squandered. Two big knocks actually. There aren't enough outfits. Each girl gets only one outfit, and one swimsuit. Should have gone full SK. But the "pool scenes' make for some fun comedy. And the white coffin outfit for leveling is a nice gothic horror vibe.

The skill tree is ok, but leveling up the gear is where it's at. Which takes grinding gold, which is why the time limit is so awful.

The story is slight, kind of like a tone poem. But it totally works. Tragic and haunting. Girls on a mission. Sidequests feel like social links and skill-boost your party girls. Two hot villain girls, some naughty torture. But it's very short and lean for a JRPG.

Monster Girls is what's missing. If it had monster girls as your party girls instead of little generic pets, I'd be a 5-star experience. But since it doesn't, the pets are mostly useless. A few help unlock hidden nooks with treasure loot. NOA1 this is definitely not.

Overall, I regret buying this full price at launch. Should have waited for $30 and a patched out time limit. But c'est la vie.

I am surprised at how polished and fun this game is. Surprised because some of the same people have developed games such as Dead Island and Dead Island Riptide. They're a pretty good developer from Poland. While those games were fun with zombies and gore, they were very buggy and had a lot if gameplay imbalances. This game is not a sequel but more like a better younger brother of Deae Island games. The game is excellent not only because of better graphics but because of the very fun and bug free gameplay. I almost haven't seen a single glitch or a bug from 30 or so hours of playing.
Killing zombies is very fun and satisfying. There are various ways to kill them creatively that helps the player level up more rapidly or gives some other minor rewards. The acrobatics and parkour aspect , while kind of unbelievable, is very fun. It feels better than Mirror's Edge because it is easier to do various tricks. There are still challenges like enemies in the way it falling when you jump without paying attention.
The developers managed to create a very deceptively challenging combat too. The zombies seem slow and harmless individually but when you get surrounded by them everything changes into a hectic survival combat based on quick responses and resource management. Your weapon can suddenly break, you may run out of medkits, and you might suddenly face runner zombies that occasionally appear.

Finally, you can craft a variety of very fun weapons. It is fun not only because of the weapon use on its own but also because there is an incentive to loot all sorts of boxes, containers, pick locks, and search the dead bodies. That and you will want to find nicer base weapons as well.

This is the 4th wipEout game i've owned and it's the most boring of the 4 i've played.
I owned the very first 'wipEout' and 'wipEout XL' on Playstation One and played the hell out of those, especially XL [which was the 2nd in the series]. I owned 'wipEout Fusion' for PS2 and loved it almost as much as XL. Played that a ton too.
But this new wipEout is pretty boring. The battle mechanic is so tame that weapons are pointless. And i miss the pitstops, which takes away much strategy.

They pretty much made this game into just racing.. what weapons/items you acquire are non-memorable.. and it's practically impossible to die because you can just keep devouring weapons/items instead of using them. In old wipeout games you didn't get any benefit from discarding an item other than freeing up your inventory for the next weapon-pad you ran across. But in this game we get fed significant energy upon discarding.. which is so stupid. because i never can die.

The only time you might die or kill anything are in those certain special bonus tracks where combat is enforced and you have to take a more tanky craft to race with. Those levels are even more boring than the normal tracks. these bonus tracks have emphasis on combat and yet hardly anything dies and the speed is slow. you can just keep feeding off of weapon-pads and last forever.

In the old wipEout XL for pso, i had to be very careful and always on my toes and there was always a threat of danger and you could strategically decide if taking the time to pitstop was worth it. In every match i'd kill at least some opponents or die trying.

But in this new vita wipEout 2048 i find myself just cruising around gracefully.. riding walls without fear of death because i know i can just eat more weapons.. and since weapons almost never are useful for killing or slowing anything you are better off just ignoring that and just using them for consumption. I've been playing this vita game for about 3 years now and i can only recall maybe a few times i actually saw something die.

in XL i died like all the time. in 2048 i cant remember the last time i died.

XL gave me excitement and kept me on the edge of my seat.. but 2048 makes me zone out and think of other things.

it is not a bad racing game, but definitely is poorly thought out and is the worst of the series, that i have played.

Here is what i want for the next wipEout:
I want pitstops back..
i want to fear death..
i want it easy to die.
I should be able to eliminate all opponents in a given match. In XL i could do that.
i want discarding weapons/items to NOT feed you any health..
i want traps back and weapons to stun or do significant damage
I want to be able to aim better.
i want to have a reason to use rear-view mirror like i use to do in xl, where i could shoot people behind me.
I want better music: the music in this game is tame by comparison to XL and Fusion. no tune is memorable in 2048.

and i want all of this in regular tracks; i dont want to play 'special combat' tracks for this effect... which still fails miserably and lacks all that i said above. i avoid those levels in 2048 because they just dont seem fun in how they are handled.

I dont understand the glaringly positive reviews for this game. those people are clearly not wipEout vets like me. i bet they just played it a little here and there and noticed the speed and graphics and instantly gave it good remarks without taking the time to see what was stripped away.

This game feels like the fisher-price of the series... i think it was toned down for kids because of online-play.. so that there would be no crybabies complaining about getting shot down.

Instead of being clever it often was more about having to do it multiple times. What was great about the shrines in BOTW, was they never overstayed their welcome, and I was consistently regretting going into a vault because I knew it would be dull. Huge improvement over the standard XB controller, especially for those who play on PC or prefer a wired controller. Extra top and rear triggers are positioned well and I don't find myself accidentally pressing them like I did with the Victrix Gambit. The Scuf and Elite series controllers also use the paddle design and I don't like any of them because it really limits how you can hold the controller. This controller doesn't have as much customization as some other models but it works well as is and I'm happy with it for how I play games. You do get 2 different thumbstick styles which are easily interchangeable. I can see some people not liking this sort of button configuration, and it's probably worse for people with smaller hands.

The texture is very grippy and may be too harsh for sensitive hands but I like it. I prefer more texture than a slippery controller and I never felt like it was hurting my hands or too abrasive for me.

The 6 mappable buttons can be mapped to any standard XB button and is useful if you find yourself using your right thumb too often. The top ones are inset sort of far which could be bad for smaller hands, but I didn't have an issue reaching them. The rear triggers are also very useful depending on the game and although it takes a bit of time to get used to them, they can be a real advantage in fast paced FPS games. The trigger locks on the back shorten the throw of the main triggers and are also helpful for shooting games where you don't need the long travel like you would in a driving game for example.

The Chroma feature is nice and adds a bit of color to the controller, especially in dark environments. Color can be customized using the free software and just adds a little extra flair compared to the normal controller.

One downside that seems to be present in a lot of these aftermarket XBOX controllers is the mappable keys can't be used for macros or special functions. They really wanted to cater the controller to work with all the XBOX units and PC is just an added bonus. It's not a huge deal for me but I can see some people wanting that functionality if they play on PC and want to program a preset combination of button presses to one button. There is an app for both the XBOX and PC to set up all the button mappings and lighting effects and it's very simple to use both of them.

One cool feature I wasn't expecting is the tactile buttons which feel and sound amazing. The standard XBOX controller feels cheap by comparison and it really adds to the playing experience having the tactile feel and click sound. The sound may be irritating to other people around you, so that's something to consider.

Another feature I didn't know about before using this controller is the sensitivity clutch. It is adjustable with the software and allows you to adjust the thumbstick sensitivity and may be useful for people who are very particular about how the sticks feel when playing.

For about 50 dollars more than the normal Wolverine V2, this controller adds a lot of functionality, especially with the mappable buttons. It feels great and seems like it was made to last. I tested it on my XB1 and PC and it also works with the Series S and X consoles. I don't mind a wired controller since I play on a PC monitor at a desk and it's nice never having to think about battery level. I also like that the USB-C cable is replaceable if it gets damaged, this wasn't the case with the old Wolverine V2. I love this controller but I realize it's not for everyone. People with smaller hands might struggle with some of the mappable buttons and the clicking might be annoying if you play around non gamer friends and family.

Where to begin? I was looking forward to this for a while, and though I finished the game some time ago, I finally decided to write a review. I won’t even touch the obvious performance issues this game had. I would have knocked it down to one star, except that the first few patches rendered the game technically playable on my PS4Pro. It’s still pretty clear there are compromises to get it running on PS4, and frankly it’s unacceptable when you have games that look as good as RDR2 or Ghost of Tsushima. The gameplay isn’t particularly special, most of the guns lack a certain punch even if they look cool. Frankly, I spent most of my time using quick hacks on enemies, the gun play was that mediocre. All of this still would make a three star game though if not for story content. As it stood everything was just competent enough that I wanted to experience all the story before I cast my final judgement, and after having finished it once I have no desire to play it again. I wouldn’t care if every bug was fixed and the graphics improved a hundred fold it. It wouldn’t matter.

The story content seems expansive at first. Icons all over the map. NPC’s calling you all the time. Sadly, most of the side jobs are utterly forgettable with their narrative thrust being delivered through the old “note found on a dead NPC” trope. There are a few decent missions for a few of the friends you make in game, these offer little glimmers of what could have been. Most of it all seems to boil down to shooting or quick hacking your way through a bunch of baddies. Then there’s the main quest, which asks a bunch of interesting questions but fails to follow through in a satisfying way that gives your choices any real meaning. I remember when I first finished Witcher III, even though I got the “bad” ending, how excited I was to go through it again. After reading the other end states of CP2077, you couldn’t pay me to play this again.

Long term civ fans may groan when an expansion appears, offerings to previous games in the series having offered little in the way of interesting play, but merely offered a few ornements like a new civ or some new units. Not so with Civ 4: Warlords. Of course this offers the usual, a few new civs like Koreans, Vikings, Carthanaginians, and the return of the old favorite Zulus, but that is what makes this a worthwhile expnasion. On the side of the mundane and worthwhile, the game now does things like dispalys the odds for each encounter when you attack, a useful addition to learning players. Of strategic interest the game gives each civ a unique building, really a variant on a pre-existing structure, but a wrinkle that will give players some food for thought.

Where the expansion really shines is on the creative side. The designers truly went out of their way here. THings like the chance to play the barbarians -- a faciniating idea that gives interesting perspective -- or highly creative scinarios such as one being the mongols in the conquest of asia where you have no cities and develop techs through conquest -- an excellent strategic metaphor for nomadic expansion.

Overall, those who did not like civ 4 should not bother. But for those who found them perpetually moving their cursor for "another chance" this game proves well worthwhile.

Even more than the last Mod, in Beyond the Sword seeks to create a sort of Civ IV.V. In several ways they succeed: the new espionage feature adds an interesting element to the game, which judiciously used can give a player a serious edge. Likewise, Corporations, though criticized by many, add a level of excitement to the late game, which often comes down to just a race, and can further individualize a players strategy. Wanting to win a cultural victory? The Jewelry Company is gives you a considerable boost in culture. Going for a conquest or space race win? The production boost from certain corporations can make all the difference.

Likewise, several of the new Civilizations and leaders added offer players interesting variety. The Holy Roman Empire and Ethiopia being particularly fun. Graphics have likewise been improved, particularly with regard to greater unit individualization for particular cultures (no more medieval looking Aztec knights!, though everything still looks the same in the 19th century and later part of the game).

That said, many of the games weaknesses remain unaddressed. Certain Civilizations still have considerable advantages while others remain near useless. Likewise, as has always been true in the Civ series, geography remains as destiny, meaning that perhaps the biggest determinant of whether or not you are going to win depends on where you begin relative to other "players" and the locations of key resources (iron, stone, marble). If anything can address this problem, the Civ developers have yet to find it.

On balance, those who enjoy Civ, especially those looking to squeeze a bit more fun out of the game will enjoy this module. One can only wonder what they will come up with for Civilization V.
